Title: Including Women in Community Water Governance: Implications for Gender-Sensitive Community Resilience Planning
Source title: Planning for Resilient Small and Medium-Sized Cities in Ghana
Abstract: The study examined the inclusion of women in community water governance for gender-sensitive community resilience planning in the Akuapem North Municipality, focusing on Tinkong, Saforo, Otwitiri, and Mangoase communities. A mixed-methods approach was adopted, involving 181 participants, with data collected through interviews and focus group discussions (FGDs). The findings revealed challenges in forming Water and Sanitation Management Teams (WSMTs). While community members understood the responsibilities of the WSMTs, some WSMTs did not meet the required female representation. Additionally, the WSMTs were excluded from creating the District Water and Sanitation Plan. These issues pose significant challenges to the resilience of community water infrastructure. The study recommends enforcing the requirement for female representation and ensuring that the required procedures are followed when forming water governance committees at the community level. © 2026 selection and editorial matter, Stephen Kofi Diko, Seth Asare Okyere, Stephen Leonard Mensah and Louis Kusi Frimpong.

Title: Opportunities and adoptive challenges of pharmaceuticals and personal care products in wastewater treatment schemes in developing countries
Source title: Advanced Oxidation Process-Based Integrated and Hybrid Technologies for Degradation of Pharmaceuticals and Personal Care Products
Abstract: Water demand and its use has increased across the globe due to increases in economic activities, human population, and recreational activities. Even though people do live with water, individuals do not have access to sufficient safe and protected water. The occurrence of pharmaceuticals and personal care products (PPCPs) in surface water led to potential health risks to human and environmental health. There is a need to remediate PPCPs from wastewater before releasing them into water bodies. This is challenged as treatment and recycling schemes in developing countries either lack the design or have inadequate capacity for the removal of PPCPs and other pollutants, amplifying the problem. The mostly employed schemes include waste stabilization ponds, aerobic digestion, and wetlands for the polishing stage, and or their combinations are lacking design for the effective. Inevitably, there is a need for innovation and improvement of wastewater treatment schemes to incorporate the remediation of PPCPs and other pollutants in developing countries to ensure ecological safety. However, innovation and adoption of the advanced treatment technologies come with a set of challenges including limited financial resources, inadequate infrastructure, and technical expertise. Additionally, PPCPs are diverse and in the environment occur as complex mixtures, coupled with a lack of standardized regulations, create significant challenges for implementing effective monitoring and control strategies. These challenges need a holistic approach integrating innovative technologies feasible in the region, research, capacity building, technology transfer, and international collaborations. Further, strengthened institutional frameworks and establishing regulatory frameworks specific to emerging pollutants including PPCPs are needed. Therefore, the current chapter exploits the opportunities and challenges of wastewater treatment schemes in developing countries to improve ecological safety. © 2025 Elsevier Inc. Title: Safeguarding Aquatic Ecosystems: Innovations in Water Resource Management
Source title: Climate Change Management
Abstract: Sustainable development necessitates the comprehensive management of water resources in light of diminishing supply and increasing demand. This review examines new developments in methods, instruments, and policies to deal with issues brought on by population expansion, urbanization, and climate change. It starts by looking at water conservation techniques, such as leak detection devices, intelligent irrigation systems, and rainwater harvesting, which maximize home, commercial, and agricultural usage and support water sustainability. It discusses advanced technologies in wastewater treatment, like membrane filtration and decentralized systems, improving water quality and enabling the reuse of treated wastewater. This review highlights innovative approaches to governance and policy, such as integrated frameworks and stakeholder engagement strategies, ensuring equitable resource allocation. Additionally, it investigates how artificial intelligence, remote sensing, and data analytics may improve water management techniques by enabling real-time monitoring and predictive modelling for well-informed decision-making. Integration and innovation are crucial for addressing water scarcity, pollution, and access disparities and building resilient water systems for present and future generations. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2025.

Title: Progressing Towards the Sustainable Development Goal: Evaluating India's Clean Water and Sanitation Policies
Source title: IEEE International Conference on Next Generation Information System Engineering, NGISE 2025
Abstract: In 2019, India reached the milestone of being declared open defecation-free, which contributes significantly towards the achievement of SDG 6 on clean water and sanitation. This article examines how India has aligned with SDG 6 through transformative interventions such as the Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM) and Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM), with a focus on their impact on improving access to safe drinking water and sanitation facilities across states and Union Territories. The analysis identifies some key drivers including resilient institutional arrangements, substantial investments needed for water security, and effective community participation in the process that have empowered local communities to take charge of their lives. However, within social-economic complexities and climate change implications, sustainability issues are ongoing challenges thereby requiring enhanced regulatory frameworks, integrated governance systems as well as climate-sensitive infrastructure investments. A combination of comprehensive research together with data driven decisions is important for sustaining achievements made so far and advancing towards the full realization of all aspects of SDG 6 by 2030. It was also revealed that there are linkages between this goal (SDG6) with other development objectives while stressing over the role played by new technologies plus multi-stakeholder engagement in sustainable water. © 2025 IEEE.

Title: ARTIFICIAL SPRINGS AS AN UNCONVENTIONAL WATER SOURCE AND AN ALTERNATIVE FOR RECLAMATION OF MINING ENVIRONMENTS
Source title: Proceedings of the IAHR World Congress
Abstract: The plantation managed by the local Saluan Kintom community in the Banggai Regency is located on hills that rely on natural springs at the bottom of the valley with an elevation above 50 meters. This condition requires high costs to lift and pump the water. This is a common problem in the development of water resources in hilly areas. Topographic limitations such as steep slopes and frequent landslides, prevent the creation of canal networks and make groundwater exploitation impossible. Therefore, increasing water demand can be met to a greater extent through the adoption of rainwater harvesting technology. This technology is recommended for hilly areas where artificial springs are located at higher altitudes than the service area so that water can be channeled through pipes by gravity. Artificial springs are unconventional water sources, carried out by capturing rainfall, which becomes surface runoff that seeps in or fills artificial reservoirs/aquifers. The reservoir in question is an earth excavation that is given a waterproof layer of Polyethylene (PE) and then backfilled. Reservoir conditions mimic the natural conditions of an aquifer, where the bottom and sides are an aquitard layer (impermeable stratum). The dimensions of the reservoir are adjusted to the discharge capacity to be channeled and the reliability of the artificial spring for several months in a row if there is no rain. The construction of this artificial spring reservoir can be applied to reclaim ex-mining land. Apart from being able to be restored, this area can also have artificial springs that can be used as a water source for plantations by Village-Owned Enterprises (Bumdes) or even Regional Drinking Water Companies (PDAM) that provide clean water or drinking water services for the community. © 2025 IAHR – International Association for Hydro-Environment Engineering and Research.

Authors: Mabhaudhi T.; Dirwai T.L.; Taguta C.; Nhamo L.; Kanda E.K.; Cofie O.
Title: A Systematic Review of Irrigation Development and Agricultural Water Management in Mali
Source title: Enhancing Water and Food Security Through Improved Agricultural Water Productivity: New Knowledge, Innovations and Applications
Abstract: Rain-fed and irrigated agriculture are key to economic growth, job creation, food security, and livelihoods across Africa. Agriculture in Mali is mainly rain-fed and thus vulnerable to the country’s fluctuating climate, which undermines crop production and productivity. The PRISMA protocol and SPIDER framework were used to systematically review Mali’s irrigation development and agricultural water management. Mali invested in irrigated agriculture across scales to decouple agriculture from unreliable rainfall, but the potential for expansion still exists. The Malian government also developed several policies to create an enabling environment that promotes agricultural water management (AWM). Farmers employ various agricultural water management practices to control and conserve water and soil. In line with the African Union irrigation development and agricultural water management (AU-IDAWM) framework, there exists operationalization challenges in Mali. These challenges include weak implementation of policies by authorities and lack of awareness among farmers, to mention a few. Farmers lack access to inputs, technology, extension services and credit. The government lacks the financial capacity to rehabilitate irrigation schemes such as Office du Niger, wherein it politically allocated land to foreign large-scale investors without the involvement of the farmers and the management agency, and this may affect the sustainability of irrigated agriculture. Wastewater irrigation suffers from non-recognition, lack of support from all spheres, and risks to human health and the environment. Thus, the government must revamp policy implementation and utilize alternative financing models to rehabilitate irrigation infrastructure, such as private–public partnerships (PPPs). There is a need to minimize political interference in the allocation of agricultural land in the Office du Niger. Subsidies are needed to support farmers with technology and inputs for irrigation and AWM. Farmers, extension workers, and equipment suppliers must be trained to build their capacity. Wastewater irrigation contributes to food supply, income generation, and livelihoods in peri-urban and urban areas. Thus, this practice must be formalized and supported by policies, guidelines, regulations, standards, and technologies for on-site water treatment and safer irrigation practices. © 2025 The Editor(s) (if applicable) and The Author(s).

Title: Enforcing the Right to a Healthy Environment in Natural Resource Impacted Communities: An Assessment of the Scorecard of Nigeria’s Courts’ Enforcement of the African Human Rights Charter
Source title: Handbook on Human Rights to a Healthy Environment: International, Regional, and Comparative Pathways for Policy Intervention in Cameroon
Abstract: Since the UN Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm in 1972, the right to a healthy environment has evolved into a globally accepted legal right with constitutional recognition in over 100 countries, including those from Africa. This right includes the need to live in a secure and sustainable environment and have access to clean water, air, and sanitation. The right has also been recognised by the African Commission and the African Court on Human Rights, and at the sub-regional levels, the ECOWAS Court of Justice. Africa’s natural resources environmentally impacted communities—such as those in Nigeria—experience incessant pollution, contamination, deforestation and habitat destruction, land conflicts, displacement, and negative health impacts, which have made the realisation of the right more important. However, enforcing the African Commission, Court, and the ECOWAS Court’s recommendations and rulings on the right has proven to be a significant challenge over time. Focusing on the jurisprudence of case law on the right to a healthy environment in Nigeria—SERAP v NigeriaSERAP v Nigeria, SERAC v Nigeria, and recent national cases, concerning the right to a healthy environment in Nigeria, this chapter assesses the remit, role, and impact of the African Commission and Court on Human Rights, and the ECOWAS Court in West Africa. It investigates how Nigerian courts have interpreted and enforced the African Human Rights Charter’s environmental rights and the obstacles to full implementation, given that the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (Ratification and Enforcement) Act has been transposed into national law. This evaluation offers a basis for addressing implementation issues, resource limitations, and the persistent power play of the extractive industries in underwhelming the regime’s efficacy. It offers suggestions for states’ political commitment to ensuring compliance, addressing the effects of environmental degradation, offering remedies, and institutionalisation monitoring and reporting procedures relating to the right to the right. © The Editor(s) (if applicable) and The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2025.

Title: DISGUST AND PUNISHMENT IN IMMIGRATION DETENTION
Source title: The Embodied State: Emotions, State Power and Social Marginalisation
Abstract: I reflect on the relationship between disgust and punishment. As evidenced in Mexico, the Instituto Nacional de Migración commonly creates unhealthy living conditions for detained migrants. Limiting access to water, toiletries and medical services, people on the move are not only dehumanised, but also often subjected to unsanitary conditions as part of their criminalisation and punishment. This chapter addresses the following questions: What is the institutional function of disgust? How does disgust relate to the implicit and explicit forms of punishment in immigration detention? Is disgust a factor determining decisions on immigration regularisation procedures and access to international protection? I argue that on the one hand daily punishment relies on subjugation to filth, making people experience continuously increasing abhorrent living conditions. On the other hand, the perception of migrants as disgusting incentivises punishment as well as authorities’ non-compliance with regulations, including international protection. I analyse narratives of detained migrants, immigration officers, cleaning staff and staff from NGOs providing psycho-legal services in immigration detention centres documented between 2017 and 2020, as part of an institutional ethnography I conducted in Estación Migratoria Siglo XXI (EMSXXI) (Siglo XXI Immigration Station), the country’s largest immigration detention centre. I also include cases documented in 2023 through in-depth interviews with civil society organisations that provide psycho-legal support and assistance to detained people on the move in southern, central and northern Mexico. © 2026 selection and editorial matter, Ana Aliverti, Henrique Carvalho, Anastasia Chamberlen and Simon Tawfic; individual chapters, the contributors. Title: Antigypsyist exclusion from running water
Source title: Intersectionality and Human Rights: Reimagining European Court of Human Rights Judgments
Abstract: The right to clean water and sanitation is a fundamental component of the right to a healthy environment. This right should be equally accessible to everyone as a crucial prerequisite for human health. However, the case of Hudorovič and Others v. Slovenia serves as a disheartening example of how racialisation and poverty can deprive people of access to their rights. To fully address the applicants’ factual and legal circumstances, as well as the State's positive obligations towards this particular group, it is crucial to consider Article 8 in conjunction with Article 14 (non-discrimination). Further, the right to clean water is not solely a socio-economic issue; it deeply affects personal life and health, including critical aspects of sexual and reproductive health for women and girls. I also propose to analyse the case under the general prohibition of discrimination enshrined in Article 1 of Protocol 12 to the Convention in the context of the constitutional right to a healthy environment. © The Editors and Contributors Severally 2025. Title: Chapter 5 Amplifying the community voices for greater access to drinking water in Bangladesh
Source title: Community, Environment and Disaster Risk Management
Abstract: This chapter reflects on the approach and learning of an innovative project in Bangladesh that addresses drinking water security issues of the poor and marginal communities through participatory research, innovation, and social mobilization. The people, living in the most difficult geophysical areas, are facing severe crisis of drinking water and associated health risks due to remoteness, seasonality, social isolation, and poor institutional links. The geophysical constraints such as growing salinity, arsenic, flood and drought, and drawdown of groundwater tables have aggravated the problems. The existing government services hardly reach to the most unserved and needy people because of remoteness and lack of responsiveness of the government departments. A participatory action research project led to collective understanding about the severity of the problems and associated health risks and vulnerability. This again built greater awareness and motivated the poor, women, and marginal communities to establish links with key actors and take various local and collective actions toward ensuring their greater access to drinking water, sanitation facilities, and health services from the relevant government departments and development agencies. © 2010

Title: Artificial intelligence application to the water and wastewater treatment systems
Source title: Artificial Intelligence for the Water-Energy-Food Nexus
Abstract: The constantly growing urban scale and productivity have brought about greater demand for water resources, and human society is increasingly emphasizing automation and energy efficiency, which has led to enormous operational pressure and renovation needs for water and wastewater treatment systems. Existing water/wastewater treatment systems have been plagued by problems of inefficiency, high cost, and poor reliability due to lack of prompt and on-line water quality prediction technique, thus hindering the resources allocation and auto-feedback-regulation of the water and wastewater treatment processes. The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) techniques offers novel and viable solutions to address these issues. Leveraging robust data analysis and processing capabilities, AI techniques such as machine learning and computer vision can extract valuable information from vast amounts of data, identify patterns and trends, enabling real-time monitoring and precise prediction for the state of water and wastewater, thereby enhancing the operational efficiency and reliability of such systems. Moreover, AI techniques can optimize resource allocation and achieve more intelligent automation control, thereby improving energy efficiency of such systems. Based on the differences in application objectives and scenarios, this chapter systematically summarizes the current applications of AI techniques to the water and wastewater treatment systems including water/wastewater treatment processes, urban drinking water systems (DWSs), and integrated urban drainage systems; analyzes the significance and challenges of AI techniques compared to traditional technologies; introduces potential improvement direction aimed at addressing these challenges; and finally gives the conclusions and the future perspective for AI development in such systems. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Authors: Liu R.; Chen H.; Lu X.; Liu M.; Fu Y.; Liu H.
Title: Development of a Frequency-Domain Electromagnetic Instrument for Underground Metal Pipelines
Source title: 2025 5th International Conference on Energy, Power and Electrical Engineering, EPEE 2025
Abstract: Underground pipeline detection is critical for ensuring the safe operation of cities. Some urban areas lack pipeline documentation, and certain pipelines have no exposed endpoints, limiting the applicability of traditional detection methods such as direct connection and clamp methods. Statistics indicate that damage incidents involving pressurized metal pipelines, such as water supply and district heating pipelines, account for a significant proportion in China. To address this, this paper designs and develops a frequency-domain electromagnetic instrument for underground metal pipelines detection, encompassing coil design and the integrated development of the transmitter and receiver systems. The transmitter coil is connected in parallel, effectively reducing its resistance and inductance while maintaining the same number of turns, thereby enhancing the magnetic moment. The receiver system utilizes a bucking coil to cancel primary field interference and employs the orthogonal vector demodulation technique to extract the real and imaginary components of the secondary field. Field comparison experiments demonstrate that the instrument can accurately identify underground metal pipelines in complex environments, verifying its practicality and reliability.  © 2025 IEEE.

Title: Jal Jeevan Mission and role of smart technologies in achieving water security in rural India
Source title: Computational Automation for Water Security: Enhancing Water Quality Management
Abstract: The provision of safe and reliable water has always been fundamental to human well-being and economic development of a nation. Developing nations like India put forward different tactics to attain water security goals. In India, a program named Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) has been pivotal in mitigating water security challenges by aiming to deliver connections of tap water to every rural house. As provisions of tap water are increasing in the country, the use of smart technologies and innovative solutions like smart water meters, water ATMs, and a cloud-based dashboard are gaining importance for water management and conservation. These smart technologies leverage the advancements in sensors, data analytics, artificial intelligence, and automation to enhance efficiency, reduce water wastage, monitor water quality, and improve overall water management practices. This study envisages the contribution of the program, i.e., JJM, in supplying potable water in the rural areas of India. It delves into the mission's objectives, strategies, and impact on improving water accessibility and quality across rural areas. It also discusses the interconnected issues of water scarcity, pollution, and management, emphasizing the need for water resource governance. This study especially emphasizes the role of different smart technologies in conservation, monitoring, and management of water, with special emphasis on supplied drinking water. By examining the literature on the JJM's role in enhancing water security, this article contributes to understanding India's efforts in achieving universal affordability to have potable drinking water and the broader implications on public health and socio-economic development. © 2025 Elsevier Inc. Authors: Bao Z.; Wu X.
Title: Study on the Distribution Characteristics and Dynamic Evolution of Green Buildings in China Based on the K-means Algorithm
Source title: 2025 4th International Symposium on Computer Applications and Information Technology, ISCAIT 2025
Abstract: With the concept of green and sustainable development, the gap of green building growth among provinces in China is becoming increasingly obvious. Based on the data of wastewater discharge, air pollution and urban environmental infrastructure investment in China Statistical Yearbook, K-means clustering algorithm is used to classify the distribution of green buildings, and the key influencing factors and dynamic evolution trend are analyzed. At the same time, focusing on the energy consumption of each region, PCA main city analysis is used to study the main indicators affecting the green performance of buildings, and the differences and connections of these analysis methods are analyzed in depth. The results show that: (1) There are obvious regional differences. Green building development in eastern coastal and highly urbanized areas is faster (such as Yangtze River Delta and Pearl River Delta), while that in northwest and underdeveloped areas is slower. (2) Industrial wastewater emission, sulfur dioxide emission, industrial smoke (dust) emission and population density are the main energy indicators affecting the green performance of buildings.(3) Economic development, policy support, environmental governance and market demand are key determinants of green building concentration. Efficient provinces (e.g. Beijing, Shanghai) benefit from strong economic fundamentals, policy incentives, advanced environmental management and high market demand, making them leaders in green building development. (4)The evolution of green building has experienced three stages: policy-driven, market-led and technology-driven. In the early stages, government policies play a crucial role; in the medium stage, market demand becomes the main driving force; in the later stage, technological innovation, resource recycling and green social system development become key factors for sustainable growth. In the future, provinces should adopt collaborative innovation, policy optimization and resource sharing strategies to promote the development of high-quality green buildings and contribute to carbon neutrality goals and ecological sustainability.  © 2025 IEEE.

Title: Minimizing Inequality in Urban Water: ST-GNN Forecasting and Differentiable Optimization

Abstract: Mumbai's piped network delivers markedly uneven service across wards and settlement types. Drawing on zonal supply records and municipal environmental reports, we quantify distributional inequality in hours of supply and litres per capita per day (LPCD) and trace its physical and institutional drivers using spatial econometrics. In 2024, citywide service averages about 5.4 hours/day; slum settlements receive 45 LPCD versus 135 LPCD in non-slum areas - clear evidence of substantial inequity. Counterfactual simulations show that modest reductions in non-revenue water (NRW) can deliver equity gains comparable to a 200-400 MLD desalination expansion, but at lower cost and on shorter timelines. We conclude with governance priorities - universal metering, zonal pressure management, and pro-poor allocation - that shift the policy lens from absolute scarcity to distributional justice. © 2025 IEEE.

For millions of impoverished farmers, particularly those in rainfed regions and also those engaged in irrigated agriculture, reliable access to water continues to be a key obstacle. Title: Analysis of the global water crisis: Illustrating regions with extreme water scarcity to those with relative abundance

Abstract: This pioneering work provides a comprehensive exploration of the world's most pressing water issues. It offers a global overview of the water crisis, meticulously categorizing regions based on their water availability: from areas facing extreme water scarcity to those enjoying relative abundance. By examining diverse case studies, it presents specific examples from regions struggling with severe droughts, high to moderate water stress, moderate water security, and those blessed with ample freshwater resources. The book delves into the underlying causes of the global water crisis, including climate change, population growth, pollution, and unsustainable water management practices. It highlights the disparities between regions, emphasizing how some communities face life-threatening shortages while others have access to surplus water. By comparing these different scenarios, the book sheds light on the complex socio-economic, environmental, and political factors contributing to water inequality. At its core, this book carries a message of urgency and hope. It challenges readers to rethink water as a shared resource and inspires global cooperation to address water scarcity. The book advocates for innovative solutions such as sustainable water management, advanced technologies for water conservation, and policies that promote equitable access to clean water. Title: Simulation of Acute Hepatitis a in Ukraine Using LSTM Deep Learning Model
Source title: Proceedings - International Conference on Advanced Computer Information Technologies, ACIT
Abstract: Acute Hepatitis A remains a significant public health concern, particularly in regions with unstable infrastructure and limited access to clean water and sanitation. In Ukraine, periodic outbreaks continue to pose challenges to disease surveillance and early intervention, especially in the context of ongoing conflict and population displacement. This study aims to assess the feasibility of using a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) deep learning model for forecasting the monthly incidence of acute Hepatitis A in Ukraine. The model was trained using official epidemiological data published by the Center of Public Health under the Ministry of Health of Ukraine from 2018 to 2024, incorporating two time series: monthly absolute cases and monthly cumulative cases. The LSTM architecture consisted of three recurrent layers with dropout regularization and a final dense output unit trained to predict one-month-ahead incidence. The model achieved a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 5.40% for absolute case prediction and 0.85% for cumulative case prediction. While the model captured general trends in disease dynamics, it demonstrated limitations in detecting sudden incidence spikes. These findings indicate that LSTM models can support trend forecasting for Hepatitis A but require enhancement through exogenous variables and hybrid architectures to improve responsiveness to outbreaks. This work contributes to developing AI-driven forecasting tools for infectious disease surveillance in resource-constrained and crisis-affected settings. © 2025 IEEE.

Title: Management and challenges in access and diagnosis of drinking water services in Rural Areas of Latin América
Source title: Solutions for Sustainability Through Peri-Urbanization Processes
Abstract: Ensuring access to potable water, basic sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) in Latin America, particularly in rural areas, remains challenging. In 2022, 8.4% of the population lacked safe drinking water, while 74.6% had basic sanitation. Regulatory approaches vary but are generally nascent, facing significant water quality challenges from agricultural runoff, industrial discharges, and mining activities. Inadequate wastewater treatment leads to bacteriological pollution. Over- extraction of groundwater, unplanned urban growth, and limited resources exacerbate pollution and water stress. Monitoring and enforcement are hindered by outdated infrastructure and inadequate training. Critical water quality parameters are inconsistently measured, and delayed sample processing compromises microbiological analyses. Education and training in water management, infrastructure improvements, and investment are imperative to address climate change impacts and social inequalities. Additionally, unplanned urban expansion puts further pressure on water resources in peri- urban areas. © 2026, IGI Global Scientific Publishing. All rights reserved.

Abstract: The national drinking water programs should address the monitoring issues that can affect data sampling, self-reporting, data quality and accuracy, as well as adequate frequency for evaluating the water sustainability systems. In recent years, there has been a notable increase in debate regarding policy improvements and their implementation. Various narratives related to water policy and discourses have attracted significant scholarly attention. These narratives cover a range of topics, including groundwater management challenges, access to clean water as well as sanitation, gender equity in the assessment of water and sanitation, integrated water resource management, and interstate river management. Additionally, global concerns about water security and climate change are adding a fresh perspective to the discussion. Natural disasters have had a significant negative impact on freshwater supplies, potentially causing water shortages in many parts of the world. Title: Legal Empowerment in Informal Settlements: Grassroots Experiences in the Global South
Source title: Legal Empowerment in Informal Settlements: Grassroots Experiences in the Global South
Abstract: This book investigates grassroots, community-led justice strategies — known as legal empowerment — being used to promote the human rights of people living in informal settlements in the Global South. Residents of informal settlements, also known as slums or favelas, encounter a complex array of human rights violations; from systemic discrimination by public officials, to threats to physical security from forced evictions, or arbitrary arrests, to a lack of access to basic services such as housing, water, sanitation and education. This book shows how grassroots justice organizations around the world are working with residents to defend their rights and secure more dignified living conditions. Drawing on original empirical research across 10 countries in Africa, Asia and Latin America, the book demonstrates how legal empowerment can put residents at the centre of holistic approaches to urban development and confront exclusionary and undemocratic systems of governance. The book encompasses practical recommendations and strategies such as rights-based approaches to informality, participation, community mobilization and litigation. Bridging the gaps between the law on the books and the harsh realities of informality on the ground, this book will be an important read for researchers, practitioners and policymakers, working in realms of social and economic rights, access to justice and urban poverty and development. © 2025 International Development Research Centre and Namati.

Title: An Investigation into India’s Experience in Reducing Child Mortality: A Gender Perspective
Source title: Sustainable Development Goals Series
Abstract: India surpassed China and became the most populated country recently. The population of India is expected to further grow for several decades before it stabilizes. The recent past has shown remarkable improvements in socio-economic development indicators for India, yet, they are far from satisfactory levels. India’s health care service provisions, particularly in the public sector, continues to face challenges in terms of both access and quality. India is one of the few countries where gender plays a vital role for one’s socio-economic and health outcomes. Thus, India’s overall achievement in improving the health of its people is certainly laudable; however, it becomes essential to learn whether these benefits are shared equally across population subgroups. Between 1950 and 2020, India’s population grew from 357 million to 1396 million; a nearly 300% rise in 7-decades, with an increase from a total of 15.7 million to 23.1 million annual live births during the same time. The childhood mortality has reduced substantially: infant mortality rate reduced substantially from 181.2 in 1950 to 26.6 per 1000 live births in 2020, and the under-5 mortality rate, reduced from around 300 in 1950 to 32.6 per 1000 live births in 2020. In 1950, a newborn in India, on an average, lived 41.7 years which rose to 70.2 years in 2020. Along with this progress in mortality reductions, household’s living conditions and other socio-economic development indicators have also shown laudable improvements; 95% of the households in 2019–21 have access to improved source of drinking water and 69% had access to basic sanitation services. Women’s literacy rate increased from only 2 in every 5 women aged 15–49 literate in 1992–93 to 4 in every 5 women in 2019–21 and total fertility rate declined from 3.4 children per women to 2.0 during the same period. Over 85% of the mothers received antenatal care from a skilled provider(s) in 2019–21, substantial increase from 50% in 1992–93. The institutional delivery increased from about one-quarter in 1992–93 to 89% in 2019–21. Early initiation of breastfeeding has risen more than four-folds and exclusive breastfeeding has risen by one and a half times and at the same time, the coverage of full immunization has increased to more than three-quarters in 2019–21. There has been consistent improvement in the mortality indicator as well as socio-economic and health care utilization, however, gender differential is persistent, mostly to the disadvantage of female children, and this is regardless of time period. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2025.

Title: Status and Issues Related to the Implementation of Integrated River Basin Management in Malaysia
Source title: Proceedings of the IAHR World Congress
Abstract: The findings of a desktop study carried out concerning the status and issues on the implementation of Integrated River Basin Management (IRBM) in Malaysia can be categorised under thirteen (13) main aspects; namely, policy, legislation, institution, financing, water assessment and allocation, pollution control, flood management, drought management, river basin and land use planning, river basin information system, R&D on IRBM, river basin monitoring, and stakeholder participation. Enabling Mechanisms In 2012, a National Water Resources Policy (NWRP) was formulated to guide water resources management in the country, whereby the approach in integrated river basin management will be through the adoption of IWRM principles at the river basin level. This NWRP is currently under review and has been renamed as National Water Policy (NWP). The key policy issues encountered in Malaysia are as follows: i) slow implementation of all the action plans as stated in NWP at state-level, especially for states that do not have any specific state-level water resource management policy, and ii) challenges in forging Federal/State level partnerships to implement NWP effectively due to political differences. In terms of legislation, the various matters related to water are covered under many separate and uncoordinated legislation where most of these laws are either outdated or with gaps and in some instances overlapping each other. In 2010, a draft National Water Resources Law (NWRL) was developed as a ‘model law’ to ensure uniformity for all states in Peninsular Malaysia and to supersede the current Waters Act 1920. The Federal Constitution has clearly defined the jurisdiction and alignment of the Federal and State Governments over water as a resource. States have jurisdiction over water resources and related aspects such as land, forests, agriculture, rivers, and water bodies. However, the Federal Government has jurisdiction over the following matters related to water resources-i) international treaties and agreements; ii) transboundary rivers; iii) transfer of water (if not resolved between states); iv) data, information collection and management; v) scientific research; and vi) setting of national standards, safety, and security. As for the financing mechanism, after the enactment of the Water Services Industry Act (WSIA) in 2006, the Federal Government is now responsible for managing and financing the water services sector while the state is left with the responsibility to finance and manage the water resource sector. However, political, and administrative decisions relating to water management are usually made according to jurisdictional boundaries that do not coincide with that of river basins. A river basin plan is a strategic action plan for the integrated management of the water and related land resources in the basin. The plan will normally be relevant for several years and will facilitate the co-ordination of specific works by the relevant agencies who shall incorporate the required works into their annual work plans accompanied by specified actions and detailed budgets. The key river basin and land use planning issues that have been identified are as follows: i) inadequate legislative support for IRBM-compliant land use control in the river basin, ii) land use control at the local authority level is not guided by a river basin plan, iii) inadequate technical capacity to monitor the implementation of river basin master plan and iv) loss of river biodiversity. IWRM, in the context of a river basin, is about the management of available water resources in a river basin for an optimum outcome among different competing water users. Thus, comprehensive, accurate, and timely information is necessary for objective planning, decision-making, and gaining support from competing river basin stakeholders. Deciding on what to report, to whom, and how to communicate the report to the relevant stakeholders is the most important step. However, there are still issues related to the river basin information system, such as those identified below: i) too much information but lack of useful information, ii) inappropriate selection and choice of information management tools, iii) lack of coordination in information dissemination for national-level decision making, and iv) limited access to the public despite of much promises and publicity by the various agencies. There are many issues related to IRBM that need additional research, especially in relation to the local context. Managing water pollution is one of the most critical challenges to the sustainable management of water resources. Pollution is increasing rapidly due to urbanisation, industrialisation, and population growth. The appraisal of the water quality in each river basin is based on the Water Quality Index (WQI) consisting of parameters such as dissolved oxygen (DO), biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), chemical oxygen demand (COD), ammoniacal nitrogen (NH3-N), suspended solids (SS) and pH. There are 189 river systems in Malaysia of which 85 are prone to frequent flooding. Flooding has become a national issue in Malaysia as the nation’s economy and population have grown over the years and developments started to encroach into river corridors and flood plains which has resulted in increased incidences of floods. The key flood management issues are as follows: i) increased incidences and costs of flood damages due to increased development in urban areas and encroachment of development into urban river corridors, ii) uncontrolled development in flood-prone areas, and iii) impact of climate change which resulted in increased rainfall intensity. Unlike the situation in arid countries, drought is not a major issue in a tropical country like Malaysia with its abundant rainfall. However, due to the natural, annual variability of rainfall, there may be some periods in some years where a prolonged period of low rainfall may affect the amount of water stored in the dams to provide for potable and irrigation water supply in specific areas or regions. Stakeholder participation is important because stakeholders who are interested in, and accepting of the water resource management system, can ensure its sustainable implementation on the ground. Title: Carbon territoriality at the land-water interface
Source title: Global Environmental Change
Abstract: Large volumes of organic carbon are stored in wetland ecosystems such as mangrove forests, peatlands, salt marshes and seagrass meadows. Efforts to mitigate anthropogenic climate change are transforming the governance of these naturally saturated carbon sinks. Scientific and market valuations of wetlands as carbon have prompted diverse experimentation with carbon sequestration projects and offset programs. These activities may displace wetland-reliant communities and add to societal equalities. This perspective paper develops the concept of carbon territoriality to explore emerging spaces of climate governance in wetlands. It moves beyond terra-centric policy debates tied to fixed and flat landscapes by integrating literature on the dynamic (sub)surface and atmospheric territorial dimensions of carbon. It posits that combining scientific knowledge of fixed carbon stocks with the inherited knowledge of coastal and riparian communities about fluid land–water connections could foster more inclusive and equitable forms of climate stewardship within biogeophysically relevant boundaries. © 2024 The Author

Title: Primary Care Dentistry in Hong Kong
Source title: Quality of Life in Asia
Abstract: Primary care dental services in Hong Kong are provided by the dental team that consists of dentists, dental therapists, dental hygienists, dental surgery assistants and dental technicians. Despite a majority of dental services being provided by practitioners working in the private sector and non-governmental organisations (NGOs), the government has played a leading role in the development of primary care services and places emphasis on oral health promotion and prioritises resources to provide emergency dental services and special care dentistry services. Starting from 1961, water fluoridation has been available in the water supply. This has been recognized by the WHO and FDI World Dental Federation as a safe and effective measure for the prevention of dental caries. There has been a continuous development of dental services by the Department of Health to meet the needs of the public. The School Dental Care Service provides comprehensive care for the primary school children. Emergency dental services for pain relief are available to the general public at government dental clinics. The Oral Health Promotion Division provides oral health education to the public. The Community Special Dental Service oversees the provision of special care dentistry services for people who have difficulty to access for general dental services. Eligible institutionalised elderly and adults with intellectual disabilities or autism can receive subsidized services provided by the designated NGOs. For people with financial hardships, subsidised dental services can be provided by the Department of Social Welfare under the Dental Grant of the Comprehensive Social Security Assistance Scheme. Through the Elderly Health Care Voucher Scheme and Community Care Fund Elderly Dental Assistance Programme, eligible older adults can receive subsidised primary care services at private clinics. Primary Care Directory has been established to facilitate the residents to seek various primary healthcare services that are available in the private setting. The Primary Healthcare Blueprints have highlighted a series of reform initiatives to formulate the direction and strategies of primary healthcare development in Hong Kong. The Working Group on Oral Health and Dental Care was established to review the current dental service provision and all the existing government-funded programmes regarding their objectives, scopes of service and service delivery models. An Interim Report has been published that includes the strategic directions recommended by the Working Group. With the collaborations between the Government and the practitioners working in both public and private sectors, primary care dentistry services have been evolving to target the improvement of oral health of the general public. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2025.

Title: Smart Village Panchayat-An e-Governance system

Abstract: This is a smart village panchayat automated complaint management system, an effort to substitute the traditional manual complaint handling in the governance of local complaints. It allows citizens to post complaints about those basic services that are crucial for public service, such as street lighting, water supply, garbage disposal, and road maintenance. Through integrating location-based services such as Google Maps, the system enhances the precision and efficiency in complaint resolution regarding pinpointing the exact location of issues. This application provides updates, so that citizens are able to track the process of their complaint from its submission and its resolution. The inclusion of mechanisms of feedback ensures that authorities stay accountable, and this leads to a loop of continuous improvement. The digitization process seeks to reduce inefficiency, eradicate corruption, and make local governance more transparent because earlier procedures-lagging and error-prone-may be eradicated. The project represents massive strides in local governance modernization for the country, thus enhancing responsiveness and effectiveness in the operations of Panchayats. The smart village Panchayat initiative is a digital transformation project for rural Panchayat functioning, creating new pathways in the innovation of local village organizations in India. Panchayats, being the backbones of local self-governments, are engaged in a large number of public services like water supply, sanitation, and infrastructure development. However, with the traditional Panchayat systems comes inefficiency due to the principle of manual processes and the lack of transparency concerning matters dealt with, citizen participation, and everyday functioning. © 2025 IEEE.

Title: Blockchain-powered DeFi: Transforming Water Project Financing for a Sustainable Future

Abstract: This chapter describes how decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols, liquidity pools and decentralized autonomous organizations can revolutionize water project finance by capital universalization, middleman elimination, and traceable and instant transactions. Title: Unveiling Market Manipulation in Eu Energy Markets - Insights from Acer Enforcement Cases

Abstract: Market manipulation poses significant challenges to the integrity and transparency of EU wholesale energy markets. This paper examines REMIT enforcement decisions published by the European Union Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators (ACER), identifying key trends, manipulation tactics, and regulatory responses. With the introduction of REMIT II, regulatory enforcement is expected to intensify, introducing stricter reporting obligations, broader market coverage, and enhanced investigative powers for ACER. This paper contributes to energy market regulation literature by providing a comprehensive review of REMIT enforcement cases and recommending measures to strengthen market integrity. Title: Water pollution: sources, causes, and effects
Source title: Current Advancements in Nanomaterials for Wastewater Remediation: Challenges and Mitigation Strategies
Abstract: Water is an indispensable resource vital for the survival of all forms of life, economic development, and overall well-being. However, with escalating anthropogenic activities, water pollution has emerged as one of the most pressing global environmental challenges. This document delves into comprehensive methodologies for assessing and ensuring water quality while presenting actionable solutions for mitigating pollution. The analysis begins by categorizing water quality measurement techniques into physical, chemical, and biological parameters. Detailed methodologies, including advanced technologies such as IoT-enabled real-time monitoring and molecular metagenomics, are discussed to provide a robust framework for water quality assessment. Sampling strategies, including grab, composite, and passive sampling, further underscore the precision required in environmental monitoring. The document also explores preventive and remedial approaches for water pollution. These include municipal wastewater treatment, industrial effluent management, precision agricultural practices, and erosion control. Emphasis is placed on leveraging green infrastructure, technological innovations, and international cooperation to address water contamination comprehensively. The synthesis highlights the necessity of public awareness and legislative enforcement to align individual, community, and industrial practices with sustainable water resource management. By adopting these measures, it is possible to mitigate the adverse impacts of pollution, protect aquatic ecosystems, and secure clean water for future generations. This study serves as a call to action for multidisciplinary collaboration and the integration of science, policy, and education to address the water crisis effectively. In recent years, the quality of the world’s water supply has received more attention. Due to its irreplaceable nature, water is stored in a separate system. Both the biological cycle and the economic cycle rely on the water cycle for their fundamental dynamics. The proportion of freshwater to total water in the water cycle is only 2.5%. All living things require water, so it is clear that this commodity is extremely important. Without water, there is no possibility of survival. Freshwater ecosystems, food security, sustainable development, and, by extension, the survival of humankind, all depend on an abundant supply of high-quality water. Pressure on already scarce pure water supplies is increased when that water is polluted. To purify 1 L of wastewater requires the use of eight gallons of potable water. Humans have an inherent requirement for access to clean water. According to the World Health Organization, about 80% of all infectious illnesses (bacteria, viruses, and parasites) are spread through contact with water. Waste and pollution of this essential natural resource are major contributors to global warming, and humans are largely to blame. It is imperative that people everywhere receive water pollution education and consciousness training in order to help mitigate this crisis. The emphasis of this study is on the origins of various water pollutants and their current distribution throughout ecosystems and the natural environment. This investigation is expected to add to the existing body of writing on the topic and help lessen the burden of pollution on our planet’s water supplies. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

Title: Changes in Quality of Living Environment Due to Landuse Transformation in Rural Areas of Ahmedabad City, India
Source title: E3S Web of Conferences
Abstract: The idea of a living environment may sound abstract, but it becomes visible in the way people live day to day the quality of their housing, the work they do, their openness to modern practices, and the steady efforts they make to improve their standard of living. In this study, these aspects were examined through field research carried out in 23 villages situated in the peri-urban belt of Ahmedabad, India. Variables included dwelling type and density, fuels for domestic use, electricity, access to water, sanitation, transport, and household hygiene. To interpret the findings, the Drivera Pressurea Statea Impacta Response (DPSIR) framework was applied, which has been increasingly used in environmental and urban studies since 2020 (Benevolo & Romano, 2021; Rosado, 2024). The results show that urban growth and in-migration are major drivers, creating pressures on land, services, and infrastructure, which alter the state of settlements into congested, poorly serviced neighbourhoods. This produces impacts including waste build- up, ecological stress, and declining health, while responses from governance remain partial. These findings resonate with emerging work on peri-urban transformation and sustainable infrastructure in India (Kundu, 2021; UN-Habitat, 2022; World Bank, 2023; Singh & Sharma, 2024). © The Authors, published by EDP Sciences, 2025.

Title: Environmental Determinants of Early Childhood Caries: A Narrative Synthesis of Observational Evidence and Implications for Global Policy
Source title: Dentistry Journal
Abstract: Early childhood caries (ECC) remains a significant global health challenge, disproportionately affecting marginalized populations. While traditional research emphasizes behavioral and biological risk factors, emerging evidence highlights the critical role of environmental determinants. This narrative synthesis aims to highlight the role of environmental determinants as a risk factor for ECC pathogenesis. Environmental toxins (e.g., lead, perfluoroalkyl acids, tobacco smoke, air pollution) disrupt enamel development, impair salivary function, and compromise immune responses, directly increasing caries susceptibility. Environmental degradation, including air pollution, reduces ultraviolet B radiation exposure, limiting endogenous vitamin D synthesis that is vital for enamel mineralization and immune regulation. These risks are compounded in low- and middle-income countries, where structural inequities, inadequate sanitation, and climate disruptions exacerbate ECC burdens. We introduce ecovitality—the resilience of ecosystems supporting human health—as a novel framework linking ecological vitality to oral health. Degraded environments limit access to fluoridated water and nutrient-dense foods while promoting sugary diets and endocrine disruptors. A One Health approach is advocated to address interconnected environmental, social, and biological determinants of the risk for ECC. Despite global reductions in tobacco use and lead exposure, the Global Burden of Disease 2021 analysis reports stagnation in ECC prevalence. This underscores the critical need for longitudinal and mechanistic studies to establish causality, quantify the contributions of environmental controls, and explore how mitigating these risks can reduce the global ECC burden. Such evidence may promote interdisciplinary action to align oral health promotion for children with the Sustainable Development Goals. © 2025 by the authors.

Title: Farmers’ Climate Change Adaptation Strategies and the Role of Environmental Awareness and Education: A Review in Africa
Source title: Practices, Perceptions and Prospects for Climate Change Education in Africa
Abstract: Climate change is a global challenge. Even though climate change affects all countries, less-developed countries and poor peasant farmers are especially at risk and have difficulty adapting. Less-developed nations are home to an estimated 500 million small-scale farms, who provide sustenance for approximately two billion people. In addition, it is estimated that these small farms produce nearly 80 per cent of the food consumed in Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa. Existing literature finds Africa is particularly susceptible to the effects of climate fluctuation and change, including rising sea levels, melting glaciers, threatened water supplies, leading to decreased agricultural output, increasing food insecurity, diminished biodiversity, intensifying erosion, drought, and flood. In Africa, smallholder farmers depend on agriculture, which relies on timely rainfall, and thus they increasingly experience the consequences of climate change. This chapter reviews the literature on smallholder farmers in Africa and climate change, focusing on their perceptions of climate change and their adaptation techniques. We also explore how various factors affect smallholder farmers’ perceptions of climate change and their adaptation strategies. Finally, we discuss the need to improve awareness and adaptation capacity. Although farmers in various African countries perceive climate change differently, the literature review reveals that they have some views in common. Most farmers observe changes in temperature and rainfall patterns in their area. They also report experiencing increasing floods and droughts and decreasing crop production. Diversification of crops, changing crops, planting drought-resistant crops, incorporating livestock into crop production, shifting the time of agricultural operations, homestead gardening, increasing irrigation, engaging in mixed farming, and migration are common adaptation strategies reported in African countries. We found various household-related factors (gender, age, education, marital status, family size, etc.), farm-related factors (farming experience, size of the farm, etc.), institutional factors (access to information, extension contact, etc.), as well as other factors (participation in a social group, training, etc.) are affecting local level adaptation strategies among farmers. We contend that farmers are the “front-liners” in adapting to climate change, and government agencies and other national and international organizations should continue their efforts to support them. Moreover, to contribute to the progress of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, farmers’ insights and experiences should be integrated in the dominant policies and plans, including coordination of education about climate change and adaptation strategies. Furthermore, we also advocate for emphasizing improving environmental awareness through environmental education particularly in this region to achieve effective adaptation. © 2025 The Editor(s) (if applicable) and The Author(s).

Abstract: The reliability of water supply resources is of utmost importance for the electricity sector, particularly for the cooling requirements in Steam Rankine Cycle (SRC)-based thermo-electric power plants. Title: Assessment of the quality and availability of groundwater for domestic purposes in Likupang National Tourism Strategic Area (KSPN), Indonesia
Source title: IOP Conference Series: Earth and Environmental Science
Abstract: East Likupang, as one of the regions developing the national tourism area in Indonesia, must fulfill adequate tourism aspects, especially in terms of clean water needs, both for tourism needs and for domestic purposes (hygiene and sanitation) for residents in the tourism area. The research collected 20 samples at two spring points and 18 groundwater wells spread throughout East Likupang District. Measurements of groundwater depth and analysis using ArcGIS were carried out to see the direction of groundwater flow, which was then linked to regional hydrogeological conditions to assess the availability of groundwater at the research location. In addition, groundwater samples were assessed by the Indonesia Minister of Health Regulation No. 2 of 2023 on Implementing Regulations of Government Regulation No. 66 of 2014 on Environmental Health and analyzed with the main physicochemical parameters, such as e-Coli, total coliform, TDS, turbidity, pH, nitrite (NO2-), chromium (Cr6+), iron (Fe) and manganese (Mn). Laboratory test results show that most water samples at all spring and groundwater well sampling locations are not suitable for use as a source of clean water. This can be seen from the results of microbiological parameter tests, which do not meet existing standards. However, if we only refer to physical and chemical parameters, most of these groundwater sources are still suitable for use as water sources for domestic needs. Title: Safeguarding Public Health: Effective Management and Emerging Solutions for Foodborne Viral Diseases
Source title: Harnessing Microbes for Sustainable Food Systems
Abstract: Foodborne viral diseases, caused by pathogens such as norovirus, hepatitis A, and rotavirus, pose significant public health challenges globally. These viruses are primarily transmitted through contaminated food, water, and surfaces, leading to widespread outbreaks and considerable health burdens. The epidemiology of these viruses reveals high incidences of illness, with norovirus being the leading cause of viral gastroenteritis and hepatitis A contributing to liver inflammation, particularly in regions with poor sanitation. Contamination at the source, including raw seafood and produce, coupled with inadequate food handling and hygiene practices, exacerbates the risk of viral transmission. Public health measures, including outbreak management and surveillance systems, are crucial in controlling these infections. International guidelines from organizations such as the WHO, FAO, and Codex Alimentarius, along with national regulations and standards, provide a framework for ensuring food safety. Food safety authorities like the FDA and EFSA play pivotal roles in enforcing these guidelines and responding to outbreaks. Emerging and re-emerging viruses, driven by globalization and environmental factors, present ongoing challenges. Advances in diagnostics, such as point-of-care tests and CRISPR-based detection, promise a more rapid and accurate identification of viral pathogens. Similarly, vaccination efforts, especially for hepatitis A, contribute significantly to disease prevention. Looking forward, the future of foodborne viral disease management includes enhancing diagnostic technologies, expanding vaccine coverage, and improving global surveillance and coordination. Addressing research gaps and implementing effective public health strategies will be essential in reducing the incidence of these diseases. By focusing on these areas, we can better manage foodborne viral infections, ultimately protecting public health and reducing the global burden of these pervasive pathogens. © 2026 selection and editorial matter, Priya Sutaoney, Priyambada Singh, Durgesh Nandini Chauhan, Nagendra Singh Chauhan, and Kamal Shah; individual chapters, the contributors.

Title: Regional Disparities in Health, Physical, and Economic Parameters: A Decadal Analysis of North Bengal Districts
Source title: New Frontiers in Regional Science: Asian Perspectives
Abstract: This study tries to capture the trajectories of economic growth, inter-regional disparities, and socio-economic backwardness in terms of specific parameters in the districts of North Bengal over a decade. North Bengal has an advantageous location, which includes borders with Bangladesh, Nepal, and Bhutan, exhibiting considerable intra-regional disparities. The region has traditionally depended on tea, timber, and tourism, but is progressively shifting towards emerging sectors, including manufacturing, healthcare, and services. Public utilities such as clean drinking water and sanitation facilities are insufficient, especially in rural regions. Darjeeling, Jalpaiguri, and Cooch Behar perform comparatively better in terms of healthcare services, education, and basic needs parameters due to early investments and institutional development. However, the growth differential between southern districts and districts of the northern part of Bengal has remained pronounced. In contrast, North and South Dinajpur lag with basic amenities and human development metrics and continue to move upward on the development ladder. Malda remains industrially backwards, relying primarily on exports and agriculture, and having the best physical infrastructure compared to other districts of North Bengal. The primary concerns of the Northern region of West Bengal are the low literacy rate and a massive unskilled labour force. The overall composite index values of major socio-economic parameters and economic growth in all North Bengal districts reflect the backwardness of this region’s economy. Title: Groundwater Management and Governance in MENA Region
Source title: Springer Water
Abstract: The Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region is an arid and hyper arid region with nineteen countries/states with annual renewable freshwater per capita below water scarcity threshold (1000 m3/year). Groundwater is a key resource in the MENA region for improving water supply and agriculture uses. Due to the scarcity of renewable freshwater, increasing demand, and stress on surface water, nearly twelve states primarily depend on groundwater as a primary source of freshwater. Groundwater resources account for more than 80% of freshwater withdrawals in six states. There are 43 transboundary aquifer systems within the region. About 50% of the MENA region’s aquifer systems are non-renewable with over-abstraction which lead to sever drop in water table and deterioration in groundwater quality. In eight states, about 85% of agriculture irrigation water comes from groundwater compared to a global average of about 35% which also affects the food security. This is exacerbated by low water use productivity within the region with an average of about $0.25/m3 compared to $0.68/m3 globally. Groundwater valuation studies indicating that the economic value of groundwater is some states ranges between $0.52 and 0.85/m3. Economic valuation of groundwater supports planners and decision-makers in allocating and prioritizing available limited water resources in different developing sectors. Also, it will help in comparing between investing in groundwater protection with other environmental matters, and in balancing groundwater withdraw with conservation it for future generations. This chapter will assess how groundwater declining and deterioration due to increased demands, inefficient use and impacts of climate change should prompt MENA states to explore innovative and integrated governance frameworks to improve the management and ensure equitable access to strategic resources for both current and future generations. The groundwater importance for water security in the region should enhance the use of innovative technologies and dedicated funding towards integrated water resources management and heightened regional cooperation. Many countries in the region started to regulate groundwater resources with emphasis on allocation, well drilling, licensing, metering and sometimes pricing. However, the enforcement of these regulations is still weak. The depletion and quality deterioration of many aquifers are increasing the abstraction costs which affecting the social differentiation, as smaller farmers are pumped out and foreshadows a gradual collapse of the groundwater economy within the region. Few countries in the region still subside the groundwater abstraction which also affects the sustainability of this limited resource. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2025.

Abstract: This chapter explores how blockchain can transform water resource management, enabling an efficient decentralized solution to the global stream crisis. It highlights the role of blockchain in water distribution, sustainability and governance, along with the opportunities and challenges associated with its adoption. The integration of IoT and blockchain produces audit trails that make it easier to transparently gather and examine data that is decentralized and cannot be altered. The decentralized structure of blockchain makes it appropriate for locations without direct access to data centers. Water supply chain management is made more sustainable by ensuring equitable distribution, preventing waste and optimizing water logistics through the maintenance of an unchangeable record. IoT sensor and smart contract integration improves water distribution tracking in real time, automates regulatory compliance and guarantees fair water distribution. Additionally, the management of water rights is simplified, enabling equitable and legally verifiable transactions pertaining to the availability and use of water. © ISTE Ltd 2025. Title: Sustainable Water Supply in Jaipur: Navigating Anthrospogenic Pressures for Geoheritage Conservation
Source title: Advances in Geographical and Environmental Sciences
Abstract: In the Anthropocene epoch, ensuring sustainable drinking water supply is paramount for both ecological resilience and human well-being. This study focuses on a heritage city of Jaipur, situated in the semi-arid western region of India, where groundwater plays a pivotal role in meeting water demands. Utilizing data from the Census of India 2011, Central Ground Water Board, and LANDSAT-ETM, the research highlights the critical importance of sustainable water management amid urbanization and shifting land use patterns. Analysis of observation wells data and Land Use Land Cover change identifies significant vulnerabilities in the central part of Jaipur district, particularly Jaipur city, underscoring challenges in maintaining sustainable water resources. The study further explores the urban–rural continuum through a comprehensive household survey, revealing disparities in drinking water access between urban and rural areas along this spectrum. The findings advocate for decentralized institutional frameworks and community-engaged monitoring to ensure equitable access, economic viability, and environmental sustainability in drinking water supply. Title: The starvation in Gaza and implications on public health
Source title: Discover public health
Abstract: The famine in Gaza represents a case of deliberate and technologically enabled starvation resulting from sustained military actions that have destroyed food systems, obstructed aid, and targeted civilians seeking nourishment. Unlike natural disasters, this crisis demonstrates how digital and military technologies can be weaponized to enforce deprivation. Drawing on recent analyses of famine and mass starvation, including frameworks developed by the World Peace Foundation, this commentary conceptualizes Gaza’s famine as an instance of “engineered starvation,” in which artificial intelligence (AI), precision drones, and biometric surveillance are deployed to dismantle food, water, and energy systems. The resulting collapse has precipitated acute malnutrition, disease outbreaks, and long-term developmental harm, particularly among children and pregnant women. Beyond its immediate toll, this case signals a new paradigm in warfare—the algorithmic management of starvation—as a public health weapon. This analysis underscores the urgent need for global accountability mechanisms, protection of humanitarian infrastructure, regulation of military technologies in conflict zones, and the coordinated rebuilding of essential systems to prevent the normalization of famine as an instrument of war. © The Author(s) 2025.

Title: Parallel Paths: Overseeing Two Pipeline Rehabilitation Projects in Southern California
Source title: Pipelines 2025: Planning and Design - Proceedings of Sessions of the Pipelines 2025 Conference
Abstract: The Sepulveda Feeder pipeline is an integral part of the Metropolitan Water District of Southern California's (Metropolitan) Regional Water Distribution System. The 8-ft diameter pipeline extends approximately 42 mi from Granada Hills to the South Bay and supplies treated water to the City of Los Angeles, Santa Monica, Torrance, and the West Basin Municipal Water District's service areas. Metropolitan initially inspected the Sepulveda Feeder and assessed that the pipeline required rehabilitation at three locations. During the project, it was discovered that urgent rehabilitation was required on another pipeline in Metropolitan's distribution system in Orange County. Metropolitan determined that the sections of pipe required a standalone, fully structural internal rehabilitation. As a result, the utilization of Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymer (CFRP) was found to be the most efficient in terms of cost, access, street-side disruption, and environmental impacts. This concurrent work was performed by a 20-person crew. Rehabilitation of this critical infrastructure will extend the service life of these pipe segments at least 50 years, per the American Water Works Association C305 Standard.  © ASCE.

Title: Application of Nano-based Solutions for Water and Wastewater Management Through Science and Technological Innovations for Sustainable Environmental and Economic Growth
Source title: Nanotechnology in the Life Sciences
Abstract: Sustainable water and wastewater management might be a step closer with the help of nano-based technologies. Efficient monitoring and treatment options offered by nano-based systems offer a game-changing way to manage water and wastewater in a sustainable manner. To ensure that future generations have access to clean drinking water, it is essential to tackle current obstacles and encourage the ethical application of nanotechnology so that we may fully utilize its potential. Transparency, accuracy, and privacy protection must be ensured by legal frameworks that adapt to the usage of modern technologies. The use of nanosensors in the continuous monitoring of water quality is crucial. These sensors can identify pollutants at incredibly low concentrations because of their great sensitivity and selectivity. Examples of such membranes include carbon nanotube and graphene oxide membranes. Efficient removal of contaminants and recovery of resources are two examples of the improved treatment possibilities offered by nanomaterials. Nanomaterials provide unique legal issues in water treatment due to concerns over regulation, liability, and approval. In order to weigh the pros and cons of nano-based treatment approaches, laws should require thorough environmental impact evaluations. To guarantee the secure implementation of these technologies, further laws could be required. If there are any negative side effects from using nanosolutions to treat water and wastewater, the legal frameworks should spell out who is responsible. To deal with unanticipated outcomes, accountability mechanisms need to be set up. Ethical questions about the potential effects on human health, the environment, and society and the economy may arise in relation to water technologies based on nanotechnology. Responsible innovation and use can only be fostered if there are legal safeguards in place to deal with ethical concerns. Cooperation between nations is crucial in addressing water-related issues since they affect the entire world. In order to promote cooperation on nanosolutions, legal frameworks and agreements need to be in place to safeguard national rules while also promoting the exchange of information. Responsible and sustainable practices need addressing the legal problems that come with integrating nanotechnologies into water and wastewater management. Innovation can only flourish in an atmosphere where people’s health, the environment, and shared values are protected by dynamic regulatory frameworks. This review delves into the various ways nanotechnology is being used in water management, from monitoring to treatment. It also gives a quick rundown of the policy surrounding the use of nanosolutions for sustainable water and wastewater management, particularly in monitoring and treatment. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2025.
