Title: User Perception and Behaviour Towards the Sustainability of Shared Sanitation Facilities in Poorer Peri-Urban Area (Case Study: Ciwalengke, Majalaya District)
Source title: IOP Conference Series: Earth and Environmental Science
Abstract: Access to safe sanitation is crucial for public health and sustainable development. The WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme recognizes the role of shared sanitation in achieving Sustainable Development Goal 6b. Shared sanitation facilities provide a practical solution in densely populated poorer areas and offer a cost-effective alternative to private facilities. However, their functional sustainability is often compromised by inadequate operation and maintenance. This study aims to identify psychosocial factors influencing the maintenance of shared sanitation facilities, focusing on a case study in Ciwalengke, Majalaya by employing the RANAS and IBM-WASH frameworks. The questionnaire components include behavioural, risk, attitude, norms, ability, self-regulation, contextual, psychosocial, and technology, which were reduced from several items within each variable using Principal Component Analysis (PCA). These components were used as predictor variables and analysed using multi-linear regression with the outcome variable as behaviour, resulting in an R2 value of 0.395 at p<0.01. Further analysis reveals that risks, attitude, and self-regulation components are significant predictors of behavioural outcomes. The sustainability analysis, based on questionnaire responses, indicates that sanitation facilities in the area are somewhat sustainable. These findings demonstrate that users' perceptions and behaviours provide valuable insights into assessing and enhancing the sustainability of shared sanitation facilities. © 2025 Institute of Physics Publishing. Title: Mapping European innovation and policy landscapes using deep learning: Technologies for sustainable wastewater management
Source title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Removal of Emerging Contaminants: Sustainable Approach for Environmental Clean-up and Circular Economy
Abstract: Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), established by the United Nations in 2015, chart a global course toward sustainability, with Goal 6 specifically targeting the optimization of water resources to ensure widespread access to clean water and sanitation. The objective of this SDG mandates innovative approaches to managing wastewater, which is a critical component for the preservation of public health and our environment. Recent advancements across the technological landscape, including the Internet of Things (IoT), Computer Vision, and Artificial Intelligence (AI), have ushered in a new era for wastewater management, offering unprecedented capabilities in monitoring, data collection, and analysis at scale. These technologies have the potential to revolutionize traditional practices, enhance process efficiency, and play a crucial role in achieving SDG 6. This chapter explores the evolution of wastewater management strategies within the context of the regulation framework of the European Union. The methodology employs a comprehensive analysis and empirical review of 5550 patent grants collected from the years 2016-23 using KeyBERT and topic modeling to identify and categorize relevant patents. We then assess the alignment of these patents with the Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive of 2014 using cosine similarity metrics to evaluate the contextual relevance and technological alignment between them and select the most relevant patents. The analysis reveals an interest in digital innovations, as evidenced by the surge in patent grants in wastewater management. However, there is a gap between the potential of these theoretical advancements and their real-world implementation since only 68 patents show a high similarity rating with the policy document. Even in those cases, there is a weak similarity between the patents and the policy document, with most patents from outside European regions. This gap signifies not just a technological challenge but also highlights areas requiring European policy intervention, cross-sector collaboration, and knowledge sharing to bridge the divide between innovation and application. The proposed framework in the chapter will serve as a template for stakeholders in the industry to better align innovations to the needs proposed by experts in the government and to better draft streamlined policies. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Title: Exploring Climate Change Vulnerability of Nature-Based Destinations: A Systematic Review of Literature
Source title: Sustainable Development Goals Series
Abstract: Climate change poses severe impacts on Southern Africa’s nature-based destinations. Nature-based destinations are critical for biodiversity protection, cultural heritage preservation, and livelihoods in the local community. The purpose of this chapter is to explore the literature on the climate change vulnerability of nature-based destinations in Southern Africa. Using a qualitative methodology through desk research or document research, a sample of 46 journal papers from Scopus were reviewed. The results illustrate the complex effects of climate change on Southern African nature-based tourism, showing climate vulnerabilities in several areas in nature-based tourism destinations. Traditional seasons have become unstable due to changing weather patterns, which has decreased the attraction and accessibility of popular nature-based destinations in Southern Africa. This is especially the case during droughts and other harsh weather events that reduce the visibility of wildlife and tourism infrastructure. Because fewer people visit these destinations and livelihoods are disturbed, communities that depend on tourism lose money and experience increased poverty. Also, biodiversity is threatened, which impacts the iconic species and habitat integrity essential for wildlife tourism. Rising sea levels and coral bleaching further jeopardise coastal areas popular for nature activities like fishing, sea diving, and whitewater rafting. On the other hand, health risks from water scarcity and sanitation challenges pose additional deterrents to tourism. However, adaptive measures, such as sustainable water management, energy-efficient technologies, and eco-friendly practises in the tourism sector, are being implemented to mitigate these effects and enhance climate resilience. The findings highlight the need for a collaborative approach to climate change adaptation and sustainable development in nature-based destinations. It is recommended that government agencies enhance their institutional capacity, improve access to climate information, invest in climate-resilient infrastructure and engage and empower local communities. These actions may help respond more effectively to climate challenges and promote the sustainable development of nature-based destinations. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2025.

Title: Enhancing waste management systems in Canada: Integration of geographic information system and remote sensing approaches

Abstract: Solid waste management in Canada faces growing challenges due to urbanization and population growth. Traditional methods are insufficient to handle the increasing waste volumes and associated environmental impacts. This chapter explores the integration of geographical information system (GIS) techniques and remote sensing (RS) indices to enhance waste management systems in Canada, focusing on optimizing landfill siting, monitoring environmental impacts, identifying fugitive gas hotspots, and improving accessibility to waste disposal services. Canadian case studies, mostly in prairie lands, demonstrate the application of these technologies for landfill site suitability and expansion, considering various environmental and human factors. The chapter also discusses using RS indices, like land surface temperature and vegetation indices, to monitor landfill impacts and identify environmental stressors. Additionally, the chapter presents methods for regionalizing waste management systems using GIS network analysis and satellite imagery, ensuring better coverage and accessibility, especially in remote areas. Challenges to adopting these technologies, including costs, complexity, and institutional barriers, are addressed, with strategies suggested for overcoming them. Finally, the critical role of GIS and RS in transforming waste management practices in Canada, offering a data-driven approach to improve sustainability and efficiency is highlighted. © 2025 selection and editorial matter, Anderson Assuah and Kelvin Tsun Wai Ng; individual chapters, the contributors.

Abstract: The state of Maharashtra is prone to several climate hazards, including cyclones, landslides, droughts and floods. Title: Innovations and efficiency in wastewater treatment using artificial intelligence

Abstract: This document explores the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in optimizing wastewater treatment processes, focusing on key areas such as chemical dosing, aeration control, and sedimentation. Title: BOP entrepreneurship and environmental sustainability

Abstract: In this chapter we explore the dual potential of base of the pyramid (BOP) entrepreneurship to impact the environment positively and negatively, emphasising the need for further research in this area. We highlight the intersection of BOP and environmental entrepreneurship, noting the challenges faced by entrepreneurs in BOP contexts, such as limited consumer purchasing power, infrastructure, and institutional voids, which can influence environmental practices. We review case studies demonstrating innovative responses to these challenges, in the energy, water and sanitation, agricultural, and waste management sectors. We identify key themes, including the role of tensions between economic and environmental objectives, the importance of social inclusion, and the embeddedness of entrepreneurs in local contexts. This chapter also calls for more research on the connections between BOP environmental entrepreneurship and informality, suggesting that brokers can play a crucial role in linking informal actors with formal markets while avoiding exploitative practices. © 2026 Miguel Rivera-Santos and Carlos Rufin.

Title: GROUNDWATER RESOURCES AND SUSTAINABLE MANAGEMENT
Source title: International Multidisciplinary Scientific GeoConference Surveying Geology and Mining Ecology Management, SGEM
Abstract: Groundwater represents a vital yet often overlooked source of freshwater, essential for public water supply, agriculture, industry, and maintaining ecosystem functions. In the context of accelerating climate change, overexploitation, and water quality degradation, the sustainable management of groundwater resources is becoming increasingly important. The aim of this study is to analyze current approaches to groundwater governance based on case studies from California, Orange County, the Netherlands, and India, and to propose context-specific solutions applicable to the conditions of the Czech Republic. The research is based on a systematic literature review, comparative analysis of legislative frameworks and technical measures (e.g., Managed Aquifer Recharge, Aquifer Thermal Energy Storage), and evaluation of user participation and institutional capacities. The results demonstrate that effective groundwater management requires a combination of regional planning, technological innovation, and behavioral instruments, supported by robust monitoring systems and transparent data access. Drawing from international best practices, the study proposes a set of integrated measures for the Czech Republic, including the implementation of regional groundwater sustainability plans, support for aquifer recharge projects, deployment of ATES systems in urban areas, participatory water governance at the municipal level, and the digitalization of data management. Abstract: As wastewater utilities increasingly turn to data to drive operational efficiency and informed decision-making, robust data governance becomes critical. At Metro Water Recovery in Denver, Colorado, the Data Analytics Group (DAG) has advanced efforts to improve data quality, emphasizing transparency, change management, and calculation management. Key initiatives include workflows for managing fundamental data corrections, tools to map dependencies across complex calculations, and the historization of calculated values in platforms like PI. Challenges remain in automating metadata documentation and expanding user access to calculation methodologies. However, Metro’s experience reinforces broader industry lessons: that proactive governance, stakeholder engagement, and transparency are essential to building a resilient, data-driven culture. Title: Addressing inequities through localised interventions: lessons from a network governance initiative for sanitation in India
Source title: Development in Practice
Abstract: This practice note examines a network governance initiative called CANALPY in Alappuzha, Kerala, India which aimed to address sanitation inequities through localised governance, by leveraging academic collaboration and stakeholder engagement. Unlike solid waste management, liquid waste management remained a neglected issue in Alappuzha, with the lack of sanitation facilities disproportionately affecting marginalised communities. Through a case study approach, this note critically examines two activities under the CANALPY initiative–Formation of Canal Shed Committees and Decentralised Wastewater Treatment Systems. Through an analysis of these interventions, the study demonstrates the successes and challenges of embedding social justice in urban sanitation through network governance. Although early successes fostered community ownership and improved sanitation, long-term sustainability is hindered by political and institutional barriers. These findings show the need for equitable inclusion to be complemented with localised capacity building and robust institutional support, for sustaining projects aimed at addressing systemic inequities. © 2025 Informa UK Limited, trading as Taylor & Francis Group.

Authors: Sun Y.; Li Z.; Zhou X.; Guo M.; Liu J.; Yan J.
Title: Energy Management Strategy for a Wastewater Treatment Plant to Achieve High Proportion of On-Site Distributed Photovoltaic Power Consumption
Source title: 2025 IEEE 4th International Conference on Industrial Electronics for Sustainable Energy Systems, IESES 2025
Abstract: In recent years, integrating distributed photovoltaic (PV) systems into industrial facilities has become an effective way to reduce carbon emissions and enhance energy sustainability. However, the inherent intermittency and variability of solar power generation pose challenges to its stable and efficient utilization. This paper proposes an innovative energy management strategy tailored for wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs), aiming to achieve near-total self-consumption of on-site PV power generation. The strategy, while meeting the wastewater treatment requirements of the facility, coordinates the regulation of the storage capacity of the facility's water storage infrastructure and dynamically adjusts the operational schedules of energy-consuming processes to respond in real-time to fluctuations in PV output. To evaluate the operational benefits of this system, a comprehensive simulation model based on an actual wastewater treatment plant was constructed, and scheduling simulation test over 720 hours was conducted based on actual water inflow and PV generation data. The results indicate that the proposed strategy achieves a PV self-consumption rate of 99.9% while ensuring wastewater treatment efficiency and operational reliability. This study provides a promising solution for industrial facilities to effectively integrate renewable energy through flexible operational strategies. © 2025 IEEE.

Title: Impact of SDG 6 clean water and sanitation and spanish water regulations on the sustainability reports of public water companies
Source title: Integrating Legal Compliance With Sustainable Development Goals
Abstract: Spain adopted the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development in 2015, making SDG 6-Clean Water and Sanitation-a national priority. Key regulations, such as Law 7/2021 on Climate Change and Royal Decree 3/2023 on water quality, strengthened water management and environmental resilience. Public water companies were required to adapt strategies, promoting clear sustainability reporting, thus fostering greater accountability and stakeholder trust. This chapter analyzes the presence and evolution of SDG 6-related information in the Sustainability Reports of public water companies in Spain. It explores how recent regulations have influenced reporting practices, and whether they have led to more comprehensive and aligned disclosures with national and international sustainability standards. The comparative analysis reveals modest improvements in the disclosure of sustainability initiatives. Although explicit references to SDG 6 and integration with other goals increased, significant gaps remain in standardized reporting, financial transparency, and full coverage of the integrated water cycle. © 2026, IGI Global Scientific Publishing. Title: Urban development and secondary cities in Ghana: The case of Sunyani
Source title: Hybrid Urbanisms in Secondary Cities of the Global South: Insights from Urban Planning and Infrastructure Delivery in Ghana and Peru
Abstract: The chapter discusses the dynamics of urban development and secondary cities in Ghana, with emphasis on Sunyani, a notable secondary city. The chapter shows that Sunyani's role as the district capital in the 1900s, coupled with the provision of transportation, health, educational and commercial services and infrastructure resulted in its growth as a secondary city. Decentralisation policy in Ghana has had mixed results: whilst it has promoted widespread participation, including by individuals and informal actors, in governance and service delivery and ensured the growth of secondary cities and other towns, it has failed to adequately ensure equitable distribution of resources and infrastructure. City authorities have largely failed to meet the increasing needs of their growing populations, resulting in the emergence of hybrid forms of provision, in which private, informal sector actors complement the efforts of formal sector agencies to meet water, sanitation, health and housing needs. The chapter also reveals how different actors influence the processes of urban growth. Based on its findings, several policy and planning recommendations are proffered. The chapter concludes that actors must fully realise secondary cities’ potential as catalysts for sustainable development and progress by addressing infrastructure deficiencies, encouraging inclusive growth and improving governance processes. © 2025 selection and editorial matter, Christian Rosen and Nina Gribat; individual chapters, the contributors.

Authors: Maji P.; Pal D.
Author full names: Maji, Pranabi (57217842114); Pal, Dibyarupa (59146243500)
Title: Nanotechnology in Advanced Oxidation Processes for Water Remediation
Source title: Nanotechnology in the Life Sciences
Abstract: Increase in population and climate change are predicted to cause a significant increase in problems regarding water. In the near future, maintaining water quality will be the primary focus. Rather, regulations governing wastewater remediation and reuse will become more stringent due to scarcity or contamination of water. Furthermore, in order to take into consideration the new contaminants that have been found in groundwater, the quality of drinking water requirements need to be raised. Only with the development of new, more advanced, and environmentally sustainable water remediation technologies will these goals be achieved. Conventional wastewater remediation involves either physical, chemical, biological, or, in certain situations, a combination of these techniques. The contaminants, especially organic materials, cannot be completely removed by the wastewater remediation processes currently in use. Further treatment is required because these chemical compounds frequently exhibit resistance to conventional treatment techniques. In recent decades, advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) have drawn a lot of attention from researchers because of the increasing amount of more harmful pollutants in water sources. Advanced oxidation processes (AOPs), which are chemical oxidation techniques, employ strong transient species such as hydroxyl and sulfate radicals. Energy sources like solar, electrical, or acoustic energy, as well as basic chemicals like ozone, H2O2, etc., can create these species from water with or without the aid of a suitable catalyst. The current state of research on advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) is being enhanced by nanomaterials. An overview of nanoparticles and nanocatalysts for the treatment of wastewater is given at the beginning of this chapter. The most significant AOPs are then discussed, including the removal of water contaminants via ozone, UV/H2O2, Fenton processes, persulfate, chlorine and NH2Cl-based processes and heterogeneous photocatalytic processes. These processes underpin the benefits of AOPs over more conventional methods for treating contaminated water. A detailed discussion of how nanomaterials are now coupled to some of these AOPs are presented. The significance of the nanomaterials’ adsorbent/absorbent function in these processes is also explored, in addition to their active participation in the decomposition of water contaminants/pollutants through AOPs. The comprehensive advantages and disadvantages of each generating approach are also discussed with emphasis toward industrial applications. To summarize, this chapter provides an extensive overview of how various approaches give rise to varied types of radicals; in addition to the principles and mechanisms of production, the economic and environmental consequences of the various strategies are also explored. The key objective of this chapter is to provide easy access for academicians and researchers associated with the field of wastewater treatment using nanomaterials in combination with different AOPs and/or hybrid AOPs. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2025.

Title: Geospatial for Good: Empowering Citizens for Sustainable Urban and Rural Futures
Source title: ISPRS Annals of the Photogrammetry, Remote Sensing and Spatial Information Sciences
Abstract: Geospatial technologies are rapidly emerging as pivotal tools for advancing sustainable urban and rural development through citizen empowerment in India and worldwide. This study systematically reviews peer-reviewed and grey literature to examine their integration with global frameworks, such as the SDGs, Paris Agreement, and Sendai Framework, while aligning with Indian initiatives like NAPCC, Smart Cities, Digital India, SVAMITVA, AMRUT, and the National Geospatial Policy 2022, with emphasis on the citizen as a crucial feedback factor. Employing thematic mapping and comparative analysis between the Global North and South, we evaluate applications in urban planning, mobility, energy, resilience, and health, highlighting platforms like PPGIS, VGI, Bhuvan, and 'Know Your DIGIPIN' for participatory data collection and decision-making. Our analysis reveals regional disparities in India, with the southern zone leading in innovation (35% adoption) and the eastern region focussing on disaster management (15%), along with global successes in disaster relief, welfare targeting, and immunisation tracking. Quantitative impacts include India's geospatial market growth to ₹63,000 crores by 2025 and AMRUT 2.0's rapid water and sewerage coverage expansion in many major cities. However, persistent challenges include technical knowledge gaps in academia, insufficient institutional support for geospatial startups, and barriers like low digital literacy and language limitations that restrict broader participation. We recommend enhanced geospatial education, open data policies, vernacular interfaces, and inclusive citizen science frameworks to bridge these gaps, foster equitable participation, and realise geospatial intelligence's full potential for resilient, data-driven sustainability. © Author(s) 2025.

Title: Existing Policies and Regulatory Measures for Management of Emerging Contaminants
Source title: Emerging Contaminants and One Health Approach: Management and Future Directions
Abstract: Emerging contaminants (ECs) are pollutants of increasing concern due to their potential risks to environmental and human health. These include pharmaceuticals, endocrine disruptors, perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), microplastics, and nanomaterials, which persist in ecosystems and bioaccumulate over time. EC management faces regulatory fragmentation because partial coverage exists under international agreements, including the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) and the Rotterdam Convention on Prior Informed Consent (PIC). Risk assessments conducted by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA), through national regulatory agencies, manage chemical substances, but they face persistent challenges in law enforcement and data retrieval. Successful management of ECs requires addressing regulatory gaps combined with analytical complication management, as well as the need for extensive ecotoxicological data to establish the required exposure thresholds. Modern wastewater facilities struggle to eliminate ECs effectively, requiring specialized remediation methods, including membrane filtration, oxidation processes, and bioremediation approaches. A full-scale policy framework must combine source reduction methods, green chemistry developments, and the monitoring of system improvements with public education programs. Environmental protection requires sustainable advancement through adaptive governance and international partnerships alongside the use of artificial intelligence monitoring systems that focus on reducing emerging substance risks. © 2026 selection and editorial matter, Ramsha Khan, Saurabh Shukla, Preeti Chaturvedi Bhargava, and Paolo Roccaro; individual chapters, the contributors.

Title: Introduction to Gaza’s War: Unprecedented Toll on Life and Nature
Source title: Sustainable Development Goals Series
Abstract: “War on Gaza: Consequences on Sustainability and Global Security” explores the impacts of the recent war (October 2023–January 2025) on Gaza, highlighting its disastrous effects on human life, the environment, and economic stability. The war has severely threatened sustainability and undermined progress toward achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. Poverty has deepened under the tight blockade, forcing people into destitution and dependency, while hunger has escalated due to famine and malnutrition. The collapse of healthcare has led to widespread disease and trauma, increasing casualties by overwhelming facilities and denying critical care. The destruction of schools and universities has resulted in educide, while gender inequality has heightened vulnerability and exploitation. Water shortages and contamination threaten sanitation, and energy blackouts make life unbearable, exacerbated by the weaponization of necessities, such as food, water, and medical supplies. Economic collapse and soaring unemployment have worsened conditions, while displacement and exclusion have increased suffering, particularly for women and children. Environmental destruction, including ecocide and pollution, intensifies the crisis as marine ecosystems suffer from overfishing and contamination, while land degradation accelerates due to habitat and biodiversity loss from bombardment and toxic munitions. The war, rooted in Israeli apartheid policies and genocidal practices, has fueled violence and lawlessness, further weakening governance and institutions. International cooperation remains hindered, leaving Gaza isolated and fragmented, making sustainable recovery increasingly challenging. Despite these immense challenges, the resilience of Gazans stands as a testament to their determination to resist and rebuild. The book underscores the urgent need for global intervention to address the humanitarian catastrophe, hold those responsible accountable for genocide and crimes against humanity, and pave the way for a sustainable and just future for Gaza and beyond. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2025.

Title: Navigating the Bio-Digital Revolution: AI's Role in Achieving Sustainable Development Goals
Source title: Proceedings - International Conference on Next Generation Communication and Information Processing, INCIP 2025
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and the fourth industrial revolution (IR) are gaining increasing significance in the Anthropocene epoch - characterized by a large-scale alteration of the Earth by humans, as a geological time period which could have started as recently as several dozen years ago. The anthropogenic alteration comprises habitat loss, global warming and the growing population. This study explores how the fourth industrial revolution (IR) and AI are likely to redefine human and environmental health in the context of the 'nascent bio-digital revolution' (NBD) focusing on machine-human interactions, and how humans are adapting to such technological innovation speculatively in altered urban and rural landscapes 2022-2030. This paper demonstrates the impact of AI enabled innovation on the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) across 22 countries, utilising system dynamics modelling, and Institutional Theory. The outcome of the study illustrates that in the near term over the next eight years, there may be more pressure on SDGs such as No Poverty, Zero Hunger, Good Health and Well-Being, Quality Education, Gender Equality, Clean Water and Sanitation, Affordable and Clean Energy, Decent Work and Economic Growth, Industry, Innovation & Infrastructure, Reduced Inequalities, Sustainable Cities and Communities, etc. compared with goals like Climate Action, Life Below Water, Life on Land, Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions, and Partnerships for the Goals.  © 2025 IEEE.

Title: ENVIRONMENTAL RESILIENCE PLANNING IN OVERLOOKED SMALL TOWNS: Examining Temporalities and Structural Challenges in Access to Water and Sanitation in Yilo Krobo Municipality, Ghana
Source title: Routledge Handbook of Resilient Urban Planning for Small and Medium-Sized Cities
Abstract: Over 2 billion people worldwide lack access to water and sanitation, with small towns in the global south being the most severely affected. Systemic challenges in infrastructure governance and household poverty impede local progress toward the achievement of SDG 6. This chapter seeks to localize recent global calls for situational analysis to inform strategies to reduce access inequities and build resilience. Drawing on census and qualitative data, this chapter examines water and sanitation access trends in the Yilo Krobo Municipality of Ghana between 2000 and 2021. Results show slight improvements in water and sanitation access and a small reduction in the proportion of the population relying on polluted water sources. Authors: Underhill H.; Sylvester R.E.; Meehan K.
Title: Water, sanitation, and hygiene inequities in high-income countries: an introduction and agenda
Source title: Journal of Water Sanitation and Hygiene for Development
Abstract: In recent years, several research communities have turned their focus onto the matter of water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services in high-income countries. Growing attention has shown that WASH problems in these settings are far more common than we often assume. The timing of this Special Issue reflects this renewed interest in ‘WASH in high-income countries’. Our agenda establishes the importance of this field in its own right and acknowledges how it is catalysing discourse on the inherited practices and ideological roots of global WASH. As a recent field of study, WASH in high-income countries sits at the confluence of several strands of transdisciplinary inquiry and praxis. In this introductory essay, we explore key terminology and trace the intellectual origins of this field. We then go on to present the 11 papers collected in this Special Issue. They demonstrate an array of approaches to uncovering and tackling WASH inequities, coming together to spark novel insights and provocations. Four common threads tie the papers together: issues of (1) (in)visibility, (2) (mis)trust, (3) power and control, and (4) the re-imagination of WASH practice. To conclude, we offer a series of provocations for researchers, with a view to implementing the changes called for in this collection. The mid-2020s are a time of critical juncture, as we hurtle towards Sustainable Development Goal 6, and normative concepts of ‘universal’ or ‘safely managed’ services are interrogated for underdelivering. Leaving no one behind requires confronting the power and politics at the heart of all global and local inequities, and WASH is no exception. © 2025 The Authors.

Title: Smart Technologies for Smart Cities: Mobility
Source title: The Role of Smart Technology and Industry 4.0 in Shaping Smart Cities
Abstract: A smart city (SC) is an urban area that utilizes technologies, like sensors or the Internet of Things, to collect, analyze, and utilize data to efficiently manage resources and assets. In smart cities, technologies collect data from individuals and devices to ensure the effective maintenance of water supply systems, transportation networks, waste management, educational institutions, libraries, hospitals, power plants, and other public areas. A SC ensures an intelligent economy, knowledgeable citizens, efficient governance, seamless mobility, a sustainable environment, and an enhanced quality of life. The primary focus of a SC is to offer environmentally friendly communication access to devices and users by harnessing natural energy sources. Effective communication fosters a genuine connection between the government and citizens while enhancing urban service delivery. A city achieves SC status when it establishes seamless connectivity through smart technologies. The objective is not only to enhance lives with intelligent features and amenities but also to enable effective communication between citizens and governing authorities. Citizens can provide feedback to the government through these channels. This chapter aims to present the smart technologies used for mobility in smart cities, including Information Communication Technologies and transportation, highlighting their critical role in urban advancement and development. © 2026 by Apple Academic Press, Inc.

Title: Israel’s Systematic Weaponization of Water and Sanitation

Abstract: This chapter examines Israel’s systematic weaponization of water and sanitation in Gaza, illustrating how these essential resources have been transformed into tools of control and deprivation. Gaza’s water crisis, exacerbated by repeated conflicts and prolonged blockades, has left millions without access to clean water and adequate sanitation, severely undermining efforts to achieve Sustainable Development Goal 6 (SDG 6): Water and Sanitation for All. The destruction of critical infrastructure, including water treatment plants and desalination facilities, has resulted in widespread contamination, contributing to severe public health crises, environmental degradation, and economic instability. Waterborne diseases such as cholera and dysentery have surged, disproportionately affecting vulnerable populations, particularly children. The chapter explores the dire consequences of water scarcity on health, food security, and livelihoods while emphasizing the need for urgent international intervention to address the crisis. It highlights key factors influencing Gaza’s water crisis, including political blockade, military actions, and systemic neglect, which have collectively hindered sustainable development. Recommendations for recovery focus on rebuilding infrastructure, enhancing governance frameworks, and ensuring international accountability. Title: Photocatalytic approach for wastewater treatment
Source title: Current Advancements in Nanomaterials for Wastewater Remediation: Challenges and Mitigation Strategies
Abstract: The availability and quality of freshwater are critical for ecosystem functioning; however, population growth and urbanization have led to a shortage of freshwater and increased contamination from industrial and agricultural activities. The widespread contamination of water sources affects over 2.4 billion people and negatively impacts their quality of life. Water, commonly referred to as the “universal solvent,” can dissolve a wide range of compounds, which makes it particularly susceptible to pollution. Inefficient water management practices and industrial wastewater disposal, which often contain harmful pollutants such as pesticides, dyes, and personal care products, are major contributors to water pollution. The presence of these toxins in aquatic environments not only jeopardizes human health but also disrupts the fragile equilibrium of aquatic ecosystems. In addition to the evident threats to human health, the prolonged consequences of water pollution may include the disruption of entire food chains and the infliction of irreversible damage on biodiversity. Moreover, the increasing scarcity of clean water resources due to pollution exacerbates existing water stress in many regions, potentially leading to conflicts over water access. Addressing this global issue requires a multifaceted approach, including improved wastewater treatment technologies, stricter regulations on industrial discharge, and increased public awareness about water conservation and responsible usage. The treatment of wastewater is critical to producing freshwater and mitigating environmental challenges. In this chapter, the focus is on the treatment of wastewater using photocatalysis, a process in which light energy initiates a chemical reaction. In photocatalysis, the use of renewable energy sources, such as sunlight, is particularly significant, especially in the field of wastewater treatment. Researchers in this area frequently investigate both homogeneous and heterogeneous catalytic approaches to enhance the efficiency of photocatalytic processes. Despite the high oxidation capabilities of homogeneous photocatalytic methods, their inability to reuse or separate the catalyst poses a drawback. Heterogeneous photocatalytic methods, which use metal oxide-based heterogeneous photocatalysts, have limitations due to their wide band gap energy. However, we can overcome these limitations by altering the electronic band through electrical potentials, semiconductor composites, and doping. The goal of this study is to investigate potential pathways for treating effluent, with a focus on fully mineralizing pollutants. This chapter also highlights the challenges and future perspectives of the photocatalytic approach to wastewater treatment. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

Title: Water Purification and Wastewater Treatment Challenges
Source title: Machine Learning in Water Treatment
Abstract: Water purification and wastewater treatment are critical processes for ensuring access to clean water, yet they face significant challenges. One major issue is the presence of emerging contaminants, including pharmaceuticals, personal care products, and microplastics, which are not effectively removed by traditional treatment methods. These contaminants can have adverse effects on human health and the environment, underscoring the need for advanced treatment technologies. Additionally, the energy-intensive nature of many treatment processes contributes to high operational costs and greenhouse gas emissions, necessitating the development of more energy-efficient solutions. Moreover, the disposal of treatment byproducts, such as sludge and brine, poses environmental risks and requires proper management strategies. Climate change affects water resources, altering availability and quality, straining treatment infrastructure. Solutions need innovative technologies, sustainable practices, and effective policies, requiring collaboration among researchers, policymakers, and stakeholders. Additionally, the aging infrastructure of many water treatment facilities presents challenges in maintaining and upgrading systems to meet increasing demands and regulations. Limited access to clean water in certain regions exacerbates these challenges, highlighting the need for decentralized and cost-effective treatment solutions. Furthermore, the lack of public awareness and education about water conservation and pollution prevention hinders efforts to address water quality issues. Addressing challenges in water purification and wastewater treatment requires investment in innovative technologies like advanced oxidation processes and membrane filtration. These can remove emerging contaminants and enhance treatment efficiency. Additionally, sustainable practices such as water reuse and resource recovery from wastewater can reduce environmental impact. A holistic approach integrating technological innovation, sustainable practices, and effective governance is necessary. © 2025 Scrivener Publishing LLC. All rights reserved.

Title: Exploring the Intersection and Interdependence of a Right to a Healthy Environment and a Child’s Right to Play
Source title: The Interdependence of the Convention on the Rights of the Child: Understanding the Relationship of the Right to Play with other Convention Rights
Abstract: In 2010, Veerman, when discussing the ageing of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC), noted that if the Convention had been written now, the ‘concern with the environment would have been more reflected in the text of the Convention’ (Veerman, 2010). Subsequently, in 2015, Desmet and Aylwin remarked that in comparison to many areas of children’s rights which have an ‘established research tradition’, such as juvenile justice and alternative care, ‘children’s rights and natural resource exploitation’ does not yet have this body of research (p. 387). Furthermore, they described that ‘the attention for resource exploitation in children’s rights (as evidenced in the concluding observations of the [Committee on the Rights of the Child]) [has] been limited at best, and non-existent at worst' (Ibid., 406). Though the right to a healthy environment is not a named right within the UNCRC, the Committee on the Rights of the Child (the Committee) has nonetheless commented on the natural world and environmental issues within its General Comments and Concluding Observation reports. The chapter starts by exploring the UNCRC itself and the jurisprudence of the Committee in the form of their Concluding Observations, in addition to their General Comments, thematically analysing references to the environment. This chapter focuses on comments and recommendations that have relevance to the right to play, in order to evaluate their relationship within the jurisprudence. The interdependence between the right to play and the right to a healthy environment is evident throughout, including, to give but one example, in a comment from the Concluding Observations to Ireland in 2016 where the Committee expressed its concerns regarding ‘households in mobile or temporary accommodation with no access to adequate water and sanitation facilities or safe and appropriate play areas (para 69.). The right to play can, therefore, be viewed from a number of perspectives such as education, socialisation and health. This chapter considers the importance of a healthy environment for the actualisation of the child’s right to play and how this has been reflected in the jurisprudence of the Committee. © 2025 The Editor(s) (if applicable) and The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG.

Title: Current Challenges and Solutions to Achieving Sustainable Solutions to Water Security
Source title: Water Scarcity Management: Enabling Technologies
Abstract: The difficulty of managing water resources sustainably is further highlighted by the interdependence of water with land and ecosystems in addition to the direct effects of anthropogenic activity on water systems, such as pollution and over-extraction. The complex interaction between land use, deforestation, and urbanization can make water-related problems worse by upsetting normal water flow patterns and making towns more susceptible to water shortages and flooding. The growing effects of climate change increase the importance of addressing water security. Changes in water availability and quality are a result of altered precipitation patterns, rising temperatures, and a rise in the frequency of extreme weather events. Significant risks from these changes to agriculture, production of energy, and public health highlight the need for flexible and robust water management strategies. A comprehensive view of water security takes into account social, economic, and governmental concerns in addition to the physical components of water availability. Marginalized populations disproportionately suffer the burden of water insecurity as a result of socioeconomic inequities that frequently result in unequal access to potable water. Additionally, for ensuring equitable distribution and sustainable use of water resources, strong policy frameworks, cross-border collaboration, and water governance are crucial. Although there has been a boom in technological innovation in the field of water management, hurdles have prevented these developments from being widely used. The adoption of innovative solutions might be hampered by elements like budgetary limitations, inadequate infrastructure, and low public awareness, which emphasizes the significance of a multifaceted strategy to achieving water security. A thorough roadmap for sustainable water security must incorporate cross-disciplinary collaboration in the face of these difficulties. Effective management of water resources can be achieved by fusing conventional wisdom, cutting-edge science, and progressive policies. A more resilient and secure water future can be achieved by encouraging collaborations between governments, communities, universities, and industries, ensuring the welfare of both the present and future generations. © 2025 John Wiley & Sons Ltd.

Title: Introduction to the Global Water Crisis
Source title: The Handbook of AI for Clean Water: Innovations in Treatment and Monitoring
Abstract: Water scarcity is a developing global problem affecting the commercial, residential, industrial, and agricultural sectors. Population increase, climate change, increased demand, and inadequate water management all contribute to the continuous loss of freshwater supplies, and water management is one of the key objectives of Sustainable Development Goal 6 (SDG 6) of the UN. Now, about 25% of big cities experience water scarcity, and worldwide water consumption is expected to increase by 55%. Moreover, over 4 billion people face acute water shortage for at least 1 month/year, and 2.2 billion people lack access to safe drinking water overall. Not only is water security endangered by volume but also by poor water quality brought on by ageing infrastructure and pollutants. Many strategies have been applied to address shortages, including desalination, rainwater collection, water reuse, and intermittent water delivery. These methods do, however, have some negative effects, such as pipe corrosion, microbial growth, and pollution potential. The agriculture industry, which consumes a lot of freshwater, has to apply sustainable irrigation and conservation techniques if we are to reduce depletion. Climate change aggravates water stress by altering precipitation patterns, increasing the frequency of droughts, and aggravating extreme weather events. Urbanization and rapid industrial development also tax the resources that are at hand. To solve these problems, an all-encompassing approach involving community engagement, legislative reforms, and technology improvements is required. Long-term sustainability calls for a stronger government cooperation, transboundary cooperation, and wastewater reclamation, among other things. Through efficient water management practices, promotion of innovation, and strengthening of institutional structures, one may guarantee the supply of drinking water for the next generations and thereby increase global resilience to water emergencies. © 2026 selection and editorial matter, Smriti Agarwal and Manoj Chandra Garg; individual chapters, the contributors. Abstract: This study investigates the potential of integrating Information and Communication Technology (ICT) into the Village Panchayat Development Plan (VPDP) to strengthen decentralized rural governance and accelerate the achievement of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in Tamil Nadu. Conducted in Mavuthampathy and Palathurai Panchayats in Coimbatore District, the research utilized a mixed-methods approach comprising a household survey of 400 respondents, focus group discussions, participatory rural appraisals, and key informant interviews. While the VPDP process enables participatory planning, its implementation is limited by low digital access and poor community awareness. This article recommends context-specific ICT solutions such as digital literacy campaigns, GIS mapping for planning, and mobile-based grievance redressal. Title: Industrial Metaverse for Smart Manufacturing: Ecosystem Architecture and Applications
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: Domain-specific progress in the industry has traditionally been achieved in isolation on discrete physical systems without considering the broader socioeconomic context within an increasingly intertwined global economy. Shifting towards a more resilient and sustainable industry to tackle today’s challenges, like climate change and the global food and water supply, cannot be solved through siloed systems. It requires a paradigm shift towards coopetition and knowledge sharing of larger systems. The Industrial Metaverse (IMV) integrates the physical and digital space into interconnected Virtual Environments (VEs) based on Digital Twin models to exchange data and knowledge, representing an accessible meta-ecosystem. While the IMV’s enabling technologies are well explored, the interdependencies between its ecosystems and network effects, including interoperability of identities and tokenized assets, of all participating systems to achieve a unified experience and decentralized digital economy in the application layer remain fuzzy. Following these issues, we discuss the IMV platform ecosystem architecture as a system of systems for exchanging and sharing resources. In particular, we investigate system interoperable, decentralized orchestration and governance mechanisms for regulation compliance, data privacy, and access control that, if unresolved, may discourage institutions from participating. Additionally, we outline the general capabilities of the IMV’s application layer and its relation to the ecosystem methodology as an asset-heavy industrial platform. Furthermore, we discuss the most promising use case categories for VEs in the IMV, such as interoperable assets, hyper customization, and cross-collaboration within industrial production processes embedded in a digital economy of enterprise creators and communicating systems. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2025.

Title: Water, sanitation and hygiene and neglected tropical diseases in the Democratic Republic of Congo: a narrative review and policy perspective

Abstract: Background: Neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) remain a significant public health challenge in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) due to its direct connection with the scarcity of clean water, poor sanitation facilities, and insufficient hygiene practices. Therefore, investigating comprehensive strategies to decrease NTDs by addressing Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) issues is pertinent. Aim: This paper presents a narrative review of available literatures and policy briefs, and explains the aspect of WASH in NTD control with special reference to DR Congo. We review the country-specific barriers to the incorporation of WASH in NTD programs, such as conflict and governance issues, and limitations in infrastructure. Findings: In our synthesis, although WASH interventions have been established to effectively mitigate schistosomiasis, trachoma and soil-transmitted helminths at the global level, they are complicated by factors including insecurity in the eastern provinces of the DRC, poor health governance and inadequately funded water infrastructure. We also determine community-based innovations, and policy integration opportunities. Title: Groundwater Resilience in the Era of Climate Change: The Promise and Perils of Advanced Technologies
Source title: Advances in Geographic Information Science
Abstract: The worldwide water supply depends heavily on groundwater yet this vital resource remains defenseless against climate change intensification. The investigation combines the analysis of climate change effects on groundwater systems with modern technological assessments of remote sensing along with Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and big data analytics and cloud computing and Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) to boost groundwater sustainability. The study utilizes VoSviewer to analyze trends in scholarly literature from 2000 to 2024 and networks between authors, co-citations and performance indicators via Field Citation Ratio and Relative Citation Ratio based on a bibliometric review of this time period. The research shows that interdisciplinary studies using technology have dramatically increased their focus on addressing groundwater stress criteria. The research pinpoints that arid and semi-arid zones represent specific regional hotspot areas because climate change impacts recharge patterns and leads to increased salinization as well as heavy aquifer extraction. The combination of artificial intelligence modeling and remote sensing groundwater mapping together with IoT-enabled sensors provides essential services for monitoring and prediction as well as adaptive management systems. The progress of sustainable groundwater management is constrained because institutions block its implementation and some regions lack equal access to technology and their data exists in isolated pieces. The research demonstrates the need to combine digital tools in groundwater policy structures alongside international cooperative efforts to establish long-lasting hydro-governance infrastructure. Title: Research on Using Phosphogypsum as Backfill Material
Source title: Lecture Notes in Civil Engineering
Abstract: This paper presents the results of laboratory and field research on testing the use of phosphogypsum (PG) as a backfill material for construction projects. Laboratory evaluations indicate that the PG used in this study is not hazardous waste and meets the radioactive activity safety standards according to Vietnamese regulations. Raw PG did not meet the leachate requirements of QCVN 40:2011 – National technical regulation on industrial wastewater, thus it needs to be stabilized/solidified to mitigate contaminants. To assess the potential for leaching contaminants during actual use, the research team conducted field trials with two backfill sites using cement-stabilized PG, each with an area of 500 m2 and a compaction factor of K = 90: one with an HDPE liner and one without. Additionally, the team created a control site using traditional materials, with an area of 500 m2 and a compaction factor of K = 90, too. All test sites are equipped with groundwater monitoring wells to collect water samples for monitoring. The HDPE-lined site also featured a leachate collection pit. The sites were monitored, with groundwater, surface water and leachate collection pits observed over 18 months. Results from the observations show that when stabilized with a cement binder, phosphogypsum can meet the requirements for use as a backfill material for transportation infrastructure projects. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2025.

Abstract: Prior to 2006, the residents of Suka Mulia and Suka Damai villages in the Seulawah Valley Subdistrict faced challenges in accessing clean water. Title: Velocity Modelling and Depth Conversion Uncertainty Mitigation in GS327 Oil Field, in Gulf of Suez Basin
Source title: Society of Petroleum Engineers - GOTECH 2025
Abstract: The Gulf of Suez rift initiated in the Late Oligocene, probably propagating northwards, and intersecting a major east-west structural boundary of Late Eocene age at the latitude of Suez City. North of Suez, extension was more diffuse but mostly focused on the Manzala rift that is presently buried beneath the Nile Delta. Earliest syn-rift, mainly continental sediments (Chattian-Aquitanian) consisted of red beds containing minor basalts. Marine Oligocene strata are presently only proven from the southernmost Gulf, at the juncture with the northern Red Sea. By the Aquitanian, a shallow to marginal marine environment prevailed in most of the rift. The prolonged Burdigalian sea-level rise enabled marine waters to flow freely between the Mediterranean Sea and the Gulf of Suez, resulting in deposition of thick Globigerina shales and deep-water carbonates. During the Langhian and early Serravallian, rapid eustatic sea-level changes resulted in pronounced facies changes within the rift. During the late Serravallian there was a significant fall in sea-levels. The Mediterranean water connection was either completely or intermittently blocked, leading to deposition of evaporites in the central and southern Gulf subbasins. Thick halite sections accumulated in the Late Miocene, and later loading resulted in the formation of salt diapirs and salt walls. Normal marine conditions were re-established during the Pliocene, but waters were then provided by the Red Sea - Gulf of Aden connection to the Indian Ocean, and a permanent land-barrier separated the Gulf of Suez from the Mediterranean. Analysis of fault geometries, fault kinematics and sedimentation patterns indicate that rift-normal extension predominated throughout the Oligocene to Early Middle Miocene evolution of the rift. In the Middle Miocene, the Gulf of Aqaba transform boundary was established, linking the Red Sea rift plate boundary to the convergent Bitlis-Zagros plate boundary. This resulted in a dramatic decrease in extension rates across the Gulf of Suez and a clockwise rotation of stress fields in Sinai. During the Late Pleistocene, the intra-Gulf of Suez extension direction rotated counter-clockwise to N15°E.As common in GOS fields, the zone of interest is below SGH-Evapraites stratigraphic section and the trapping mechanism is structural trap, and the main producing reservoirs are Miocene clastics reservoirs, the late Cenozoic Gulf of Suez basin is one of the best exposed and studied examples of a continental rift. Several recent models of rift geometry and evolution have relied heavily on data and concepts derived here (e.g., Bosworth, 1994; Bosence, 1998). The Gulf of Suez was the first rift basin in which large-scale, along-axis segmentation into subbasins by accommodation zones was clearly recognised (Moustafa, 1976), has served as one of the premier models for Miocene carbonate platform development (James et al., 1988; Burchette, 1988; Cross et al., 1998), and is recognised as a superb example of the interplay between sedimentation and extensional fault development (Gawthorpe et al., 1997; Sharp et al., 2000 a, b). Recent studies evaluated the relative roles of hard- and soft-transfer in intra-basin fault linkage, and the significance of pre-rift structures in controlling the style of linkage (McClay et al., 1998; McClay and Khalil, 1998; Younes and McClay, 1998). The Gulf of Suez is also one of the best examples of the integration of outcrop and subsurface data to enhance hydrocarbon exploration and exploitation (Gawthorpe et al., 1990; Patton et al., 1994; Sharp et al., 2000 a, b). Despite these positive and important developments, we believe that two issues have not been satisfactorily addressed. First, no comprehensive analysis and integration of all areas of the rift has been published, in spite of abundant new stratigraphic and structural data for parts of the basin (e.g., Richardson and Arthur, 1988; Hughes et al., 1992; Patton et al., 1994; Bosworth, 1995; McClay et al., 1998). Specifically, the major differences in the tectonostratigraphic histories of the southern and central rift basins have never been adequately addressed. Second, despite the use of many aspects of outcrop and subsurface geology of this basin as a model for other rift settings, this extrapolation has not considered all the dominant factors that controlled overall evolution of the Gulf. Some of these factors, such as the activation of the Aqaba transform boundary, are actually specific to the geographical and temporal position of the basin, and may make some aspects of this rift unsuitable for a general model. Structurally The NW-trending Gulf of Suez is about 300 km long, and the complete rift basin, including the on-shore border fault systems, varies in width from about 50 km at its northern end to about 90 km at its southern end where it merges with the Red Sea, this has been traditionally referred to as the "Clysmic" rift, after the ancient Roman settlement of Clysma that occupied the present site of the city of Suez (Hume, 1921; Robson, 1971). The rift is characterised by a zigzag fault pattern, composed of N-S to NNE-SSW, E-W and NW-SE striking extensional fault systems both at the rift borders and within the rift basins (Garfunkel and Bartov, 1977; Jarrige et al., 1986; Moretti and Chénet, 1987; Colletta et al., 1988; Meshref, 1990; Moustafa, 1993; Patton et al., 1994; Schutz, 1994; Bosworth, 1995; Montenat et al., 1998; McClay et al., 1998). Title: Kuwait at the Crossroads: The Interplay of Climate, Migration and Water Scarcity Dynamics
Source title: Geoeconomics of the Sustainable Development Goals
Abstract: Recent studies have predicted that around 60% of the global population will soon face challenges in accessing fresh water, underscoring the urgent need for sustainable water management practices. This chapter combines insights from various studies to explore the escalating impact of climate change-induced migration on water scarcity, specifically in the case of Kuwait. Kuwait, a nation with limited water resources in an arid environment, heavily depends on oil to desalinate seawater. Climate change-induced migration patterns are worsening water scarcity in Kuwait, mainly due to population growth and migration, heightening the demand for freshwater. If this demand is not controlled, it could strain water supplies and existing systems, leading to fluctuations in capacity and increased water demand for consumption, services, and energy. This unregulated demand depletes freshwater reserves and contributes to environmental degradation, further worsening water availability and the country’s water stability. Despite Kuwait’s proactive measures, such as the latest desalination technologies and investments in global techniques, the combined effects of climate change, migration, and regional tension pose a significant threat to water security. The findings of this research highlight the urgent need for regional cooperation, advanced water management technologies, and strong governance to ensure sustainable water access. These measures align with the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals and can effectively alleviate global water scarcity issues. © 2025 selection and editorial matter, Lucía Morales, Bernadette Andreosso-O’Callaghan and Daniel Rajmil; individual chapters, the contributors.

Title: Water Sowing and Harvesting Tourism: An Educational and Water Conservation Experience in Manglaralto, Ecuador
Source title: CEUR Workshop Proceedings
Abstract: The commune of Manglaralto, Santa Elena (Ecuador), is a coastal town that relies exclusively on the Manglaralto aquifer for its local water supply and tourist flow. Faced with the risks of overexploitation and saline intrusion, the community has implemented an artificial recharge system using a technical-artisanal dam (tape), generating water benefits as well as spontaneous educational and recreational uses. The site is considered a site of geological interest due to its hydrogeological characteristics and has been designated an Ecohydrology Demonstration Site by UNESCO. However, this experience has not yet been systematized for inclusion in the area’s tourism agenda. The objective of this research is to propose tourism strategies integrating elements of geodiversity, environmental education, and community conservation of the aquifer to strengthen local sustainable tourism. The methodological design included: i) baseline diagnosis, ii) SWOT analysis with community and technicians, and iii) a tourism proposal for the site (route and guidelines for education-culture-environment-society-economy-governance). As a result, a guided experience based on the Manglaralto river-aquifer system is proposed, the "Water Route", which includes visits to five points of interest: a) Manglaralto Water Board headquarters, 2) historic wells 1 and 2, c) technical-artisanal dam site, e) water reservoirs and natural viewpoint, and f) Manglaralto river mouth, where technical and historical information on community water management, its benefits, and local significance can be obtained. This research allows for the revaluation of the underground resource and the infrastructure for rescuing ancestral knowledge with Water Sowing and Harvesting (WS&H) systems, integrating its educational (social-cultural-environmental) and tourist (administration-operation) use as a social innovation project. © 2025 Copyright for this paper by its authors.

Title: Where Commitment Meets Innovation: Transforming EJ Commitment into Tangible Impact
Source title: Proceedings - WEFTEC 2025: 98th Water Environment Federation Technical Exhibition and Conference
Abstract: The Northeast Ohio Regional Sewer District (“the District”) provides wastewater and stormwater services to more than 1 million Northeast Ohioans every day. In 2022, the District published our Environmental Justice (EJ) Commitment Statement, clarifying how EJ has always resonated with our mission and establishing guideposts to help us reflect upon the effectiveness of our efforts. The “EJ in Action” and “Environmental Justice Resource Guide” tools have since been developed in-house to bring EJ to a tangible level and provide actionable guidance for each of the nearly 800 District employees. This paper offers an example of how a utility can activate employees at every level beyond commitment and discussion of Environmental Justice into a space of meaningful action and engagement that has tangible impact on their service area. The District defines EJ as follows: “through meaningful engagement, informed actions, and equitable treatment, the District will continue to provide equitable treatment and meaningful engagement of our residents—inclusive of all races, cultures, lifestyles, neighborhoods, and incomes—so we may advance our clean-water work without placing disproportionate environmental or fiscal burdens on those we serve.” Environmental Justice has always been inherent to and a part of District work. At the most basic level, we serve an EJ role by treating wastewater, reducing or eliminating combined sewer overflow (CSO) pollution, and addressing stormwater flooding and erosion. For example, on a recent Engineering & Construction Department (E&C) CSO Control project, the Kingsbury Run Consolidation Sewer, realignment of one of the tunnels will reduce impact to residents in a low-income neighborhood both during construction and future operation and maintenance, and also save costs through improved constructability of the tunnel. The realignment can be viewed solely as technical enhancement, but through the EJ lens this is a tangible example of informed action and equitable treatment at work to reduce potential environmental or fiscal burden. This example was discussed at an E&C All-Department meeting in an effort to bring EJ from a conceptual level to a practical one. E&C staff were eager to have additional examples highlighted to further their knowledge. From this feedback was born the “EJ in Action” database. This tool helps identify, track, and communicate EJ opportunities in the planning, design, and construction of E&C projects. Examples are submitted by employees, who are then given the opportunity to present about their example in future departmental meetings—a combination of ongoing departmental learning and professional development in one. After successful rollout to the E&C department, the tool will be expanded in 2025 to include District-wide examples as part of NEORSD’s 2025-27 Strategic Plan. Building familiarity with EJ is a first step for many employees, but soon deeper questions emerge. What tools or guidance exist that help employees ensure EJ is woven into their work in a more meaningful way than a simple “add-on” or check box? How can we ensure the core connection to EJ is being made across all facets of our work as a utility: project management, communication, operation and maintenance, field services, and finance…to name just a few. This deeper question and request for guidance is being answered by the District’s “Environmental Justice Resource Guide.” This comprehensive document, developed by staff across the District, provides brainstorming prompts, communication frameworks, a digital hub of geo-referenced data to visualize and measure EJ in project areas, and suggestions for best practices to help ensure EJ is a key component in every project. The document is currently being finalized by the Environmental Justice Committee and will be rolled out for District-wide use and reference by the end of 2025. Title: IoT-Based Smart Hydroponics for Automated Nutrient, Climate, Irrigation, and Health Monitoring
Source title: 2025 International Electronics Symposium, IES 2025
Abstract: This study presents HydroNutraLeaf as a selfgoverning hydroponic tower system built with Internet of Things technology to automate the critical aspects of hydroculture farming by uniting water supply management with environmental control and watering systems and plant health monitoring capabilities. The system unites multiple essential components to operate as one unit. The system incorporates an automatic plant disease detection system through real-time image acquisition which uses Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) algorithms and cloud-based warning protocols for classification purposes. An automated system comprising Raspberry Pi actuators, NPK sensors, and machine learning functions delivers nutrients at proper stages during plant growth. A reinforcement learning system directs the management of climate factors including temperature and humidity together with Light Emitting Diode (LED) spectrums to achieve superior yield production and product quality. The system includes a self-operated irrigation system with Electrical Conductivity (EC), potential of hydrogen (pH) regulation features which utilizes SVM-based prediction methods in combination with real-time monitoring to achieve optimum root environment conditions. Users can access a dashboard in Grafana to monitor and control the system by using cloud platforms which include Firebase and AWS. The experimental findings reveal water consumption decreased by 30% along with improved nutritional efficiency reaching 25% and enhanced crop yield reaching 15% with better health performance. The sustainable farming operations and commercial greenhouse implementation benefit from HydroNutraLeaf solution which operates through a scalable model based on data analysis and requires minimal human intervention. © 2025 IEEE.

Title: Future directions in water quality management: integrating advanced technologies and sustainable practices
Source title: Computational Automation for Water Security: Enhancing Water Quality Management
Abstract: To meet the mounting difficulties of pollution, shortage, and climate change related to water, future trends and developing technologies in water quality management will help in enhancing monitoring, treatment, and conservation efforts. Deployment of remote monitoring systems and sensor networks should continuously monitor several water quality parameters and pollutants in real time. Creation of intelligent sensors and Internet of Things (IoT) gadgets with sophisticated analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms for data processing and early identification of problems with water quality can play a significant role in water quality management. Using analytics systems to evaluate vast amounts of data on water quality for trend analysis, pattern recognition, and predictive modeling from a variety of sources, such as sensors, satellites, and citizen science projects, can enhance the technology to a significant level. AI and machine learning approaches can be utilized to predict water quality measurements and sources of pollution, which at the end enhance treatment procedures using real-time inputs and previous data. Application of decentralized water treatment systems for the localized treatment of contaminated water sources and wastewater, such as advanced oxidation processes, electrocoagulation, and small-scale membrane filtration, can become very much helpful in future days. Creation of off-grid and solar-powered water treatment systems can be used to lessen dependency on centralized infrastructure and supply of safe drinking water in isolated and resource-constrained locations. Investigation of biological remediation methods for the removal and degradation of nutrient compounds and organic contaminants from water bodies may include methods like phytoremediation and bioaugmentation. Application of nutrient recovery technology can be done to recover valuable resources from wastewater streams and advance a circular economy strategy, such as nutrient extraction from wastewater and algae cultivation for biofuel production. Water infrastructure should be designed and renovated to endure extreme weather, flooding, and sea level rise. Natural solutions including green infrastructure, wetlands restoration, and natural flood control should be incorporated. To improve the resilience and sustainability of water resources in a changing climate, water quality management techniques should be integrated with initiatives to mitigate climate change, such as carbon sequestration in aquatic ecosystems and adoption of integrated approaches to water resource management that encourage multi-stakeholder cooperation, adaptive governance, and democratic decision-making while considering the interdependence of water quality, quantity, and ecosystem health. © 2025 Elsevier Inc. Title: Smart Vision Guided Table Sanitization System With Iot Integration for High-Traffic Dining Environments
Source title: 2025 IEEE Pune Section International Conference, PuneCon 2025
Abstract: The procedures of table cleaning in high-traffic communal dining environments, such as temples, cafeterias, and institutional canteens, remain labour-intensive and inefficient, particularly during peak hours. While some automated or robotic cleaning systems have been explored, they often lack real-time contamination detection, and they are not tailored for the stringent hygiene requirements of such facilities. To address these limitations, this research presents an IoT-enabled table cleaning system that integrates real-time image processing with precise motor control for autonomous operation. The proposed architecture features a dual-controller setup, where the ESP32 microcontroller performs continuous image acquisition, contamination detection, manages BLE and Wi-Fi communication, and controls the cleaning mechanism and fluid dispensing mechanism. The system uses an ESP32-CAM module for capturing both pre- and post-cleaning images, enabling autonomous assessment of table cleanliness and re-cleaning if necessary. To detect objects and human presence, the ESP32-CAM is utilized. This ensures that cleaning only occurs when tables are unoccupied and free of obstructions. A fluid-level sensor in the spray reservoir and an under-table waste bin enhance both safety and operational reliability. Data on cleaning status and environmental conditions can be shared in real-time on cloud servers, supporting centralised monitoring and maintenance. Experimental evaluation demonstrates the system's high detection accuracy, cleaning efficiency with various debris types, and reliable communication across multiple tables. By enabling automated, verifiable, and remotely monitored table sanitation, the proposed system reduces manual labour, improves hygiene standards, and offers a scalable, sustainable solution for modern large-scale dining facilities. © 2025 IEEE.

Title: Prevention and Control Strategies for Swine Zoonoses
Source title: Emerging Zoonotic Threats from Swine: A Public Health Perspective
Abstract: Swine zoonoses, caused by pathogens such as bacteria, viruses, and parasites, pose significant public health and economic risks, particularly in regions with intensive pig farming. Key zoonotic diseases include brucellosis, leptospirosis, salmonellosis, and influenza. Despite advancements in pathogen control, the persistence of zoonotic pathogens and increasing antimicrobial resistance necessitate robust biosecurity, vaccination, and surveillance measures. Biosecurity practices, including controlled farm access, visitor management, and quarantine protocols, are critical for preventing disease transmission and reducing antibiotic use. Vaccination complements these measures by preserving herd health and minimizing zoonotic outbreaks. Surveillance systems enable early detection and effective management of diseases, supported by diagnostic tools, comprehensive health screenings, and accurate record-keeping. Additionally, vector control strategies targeting rodents, insects, and other carriers are essential to mitigate pathogen transmission. These integrated approaches align with the One Health framework, emphasizing the interconnectedness of animal, human, and environmental health, to ensure sustainable swine production and protect public health. Preventing disease in pig farms requires vector control, sanitation, biosecurity, and waste management. Key measures include integrated pest management, proper hygiene, manure handling, and regular cleaning. Biosecurity protocols and staff training ensure early disease detection and control. Effective waste management and compliance with environmental regulations minimize health risks and promote sustainability. © 2025 The Editor(s) (if applicable) and The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd.
