Title: Repurposing a traditional water resources management tool for the sanitation sector
Source title: Water Remediation Methods and Wastewater Treatment
Abstract: The sanitation sector faces challenges, including inadequate infrastructure, resource constraints, and fragmented governance. This article explores the potential of repurposing Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) tools, traditionally used in the water sector, to address these issues. By leveraging IWRM principles—such as integrated planning, stakeholder participation, and adaptive management—this study proposes a framework to improve sanitation systems' efficiency, sustainability, and resilience. The article reviews recent literature (2016-24), identifies gaps, and presents case studies, including Singapore's NEWater Program and Nairobi's fecal sludge-to-energy initiatives, to demonstrate the applicability of IWRM tools in sanitation. Findings suggest that repurposing IWRM tools can enhance wastewater management, resource recovery, and equitable service delivery, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This study contributes by providing a comprehensive framework for integrating IWRM tools into sanitation systems, offering practical insights for policymakers and practitioners. The article concludes with recommendations for future research and practice, emphasizing the potential of smart sanitation systems and the circular economy to advance sustainable sanitation. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Title: Risk management and safety auditing in anaerobic digestion: Driving operational excellence
Source title: Anaerobic Digestion for Bioenergy: Emerging Technologies and Strategies for Bioenergy and Bioproduct Innovation
Abstract: Anaerobic digestion (AD) has emerged as a game-changing technology, revolutionizing renewable energy generation and sustainable waste management by unlocking the energy potential of organic waste streams. By converting organic matter such as agricultural residues, industrial process by-products, and municipal biosolids into biogas and nutrient-rich digestate, AD provides significant environmental and economic benefits. However, the safe and efficient operation of AD facilities requires rigorous auditing procedures and robust safety standards tailored to specific contexts. These operations require a cohesive approach, integrating thorough auditing practices, comprehensive safety protocols, and advanced technological tools to streamline processes, minimize risks, and enhance overall reliability. Challenges vary across agricultural, industrial, and municipal AD systems. Agricultural systems often face seasonal feedstock variability and nutrient management demands, industrial systems must manage uniform but large-volume waste streams under stringent workplace regulations, and municipal systems require integration with sludge stabilization and odor control protocols. These diverse needs demand tailored audits to address feedstock characteristics, regulatory compliance, and operational scalability. Effective compliance and risk management frameworks rooted in ISO standards, Hazard and Operability (HAZOP) studies, and structured emergency action plans enable facilities to safeguard worker safety, maintain environmental integrity, and ensure process stability. AD facilities face numerous safety challenges, including the risks of drowning and falls near open tanks, as well as biogas-related hazards such as asphyxiation and fire. Addressing these dangers requires confined space entry protocols, robust electrical system safeguards, and comprehensive safety measures that tackle chemical, mechanical, and thermal risks. Employing protective equipment, enforcing lockout/tagout procedures, and utilizing real-time hazard monitoring systems are essential practices that enhance safety and mitigate risks effectively. Predictive maintenance, artificial intelligence (AI), and immersive training platforms play pivotal roles in reinforcing proactive safety cultures within AD operations. These technologies interact by providing real-time data insights, automating adjustments to process variables, and enhancing workforce preparedness through realistic simulations, creating a cohesive framework for safety and efficiency. These technologies, combined with best practices and case studies, reveal tangible benefits, including improved biogas yields, reduced downtime, and stronger community relations. Through the integration of rigorous auditing processes and advanced technologies, AD operators can unlock the full potential of the process, driving innovation, enhancing sustainability, and paving the way for a resilient and cleaner future. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Bridging the Health Divide: A Policy Perspective on Indigenous Healthcare in Bangladesh
Source title: Health Science Reports
Abstract: Background: Indigenous populations in Bangladesh—often referred to as Adibashi or Upojati—experience persistent health disparities. Geographic isolation, linguistic and cultural exclusion, and poverty drive these disparities. These communities, estimated at over two million, report considerably higher rates of maternal mortality, undernutrition, and limited access to institutional healthcare. This situation persists despite constitutional protections and national development goals. Objective: This perspective examines the structural, cultural, and policy-level barriers to healthcare access among Bangladesh's tribal communities. It also proposes evidence-based, inclusive strategies designed to achieve health equity. Methods: A narrative review approach was guided by the SANRA checklist. Literature was identified through PubMed, Google Scholar, and government portals. Sources included national surveys, ethnographic studies, and comparative policy models from Canada, Nepal, and the Philippines. Key themes analyzed were infrastructure deficits, workforce shortages, traditional medicine, linguistic barriers, and WASH access. A SWOT framework synthesizes insights and informs recommendations. Key Findings: Tribal health inequities in Bangladesh stem from weak infrastructure, cultural exclusion, workforce shortages, and poor health governance. International models show the benefits of decentralized, culturally adapted, community-led care. Conclusion: Achieving SDG 3 for indigenous populations requires urgent political commitment, targeted investment, and inclusive planning. Priorities include the establishment of a Tribal Health Desk, integration of traditional medicine, mobile health delivery, and culturally adapted training. Advancing indigenous health equity aligns with constitutional commitments and global standards of public health justice. © 2025 The Author(s). Title: Water and wastewater applications in developed and developing countries: extant experience and plan for the future
Source title: Water Remediation Methods and Wastewater Treatment
Abstract: Water and wastewater management are crucial for sustaining growing populations while ensuring environmental sustainability. Developed nations benefit from advanced infrastructure, robust regulatory frameworks, and cutting-edge technologies such as membrane filtration, desalination, and wastewater reuse. These measures enhance water efficiency and sustainability, particularly in water-scarce regions. In contrast, developing countries struggle with inadequate infrastructure, financial limitations, and rapid urbanization, resulting in water pollution and limited clean water access. However, emerging solutions such as decentralized treatment systems, rainwater harvesting, and affordable filtration technologies offer promising alternatives, though they require more substantial policy support and investment to scale effectively. In modern water management, technological advancements function critically. The artificial intelligence, internet of things, and big data analytics optimize water distribution and treatment in developed nations, thereby improving efficiency and reducing losses. Meanwhile, resource-limited regions increasingly adopt cost-effective technologies like solar desalination and small-scale filtration systems to enhance water security. Governance and policy frameworks significantly impact water management, with strong institutions and enforcement ensuring sustainability in developed nations. In contrast, weak governance, corruption, and political instability often hinder progress in developing countries. Climate change further complicates water security, exacerbating worldwide droughts, floods, and water stress. Adaptive strategies such as circular economy models, integrated water resource management, and sustainable financing mechanisms are essential for long-term resilience. This chapter highlights the significance of innovation, policy reform, and international cooperation in bridging the gap between developing and developed nations.
